articles.title: William Contreras leads charge as Brewers chase Yoshinobu Yamamoto, take 2-0 NLCS lead over Dodgers
articles.summary: The pitchers' duel we were promised on Monday never materialized.
articles.body: The pitchers' duel we were promised on Monday never materialized.The Milwaukee Brewers and Los Angeles Dodgers each scored a first-inning run in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series in a precursor to what became a relative slugfest. Thanks to a big game at the plate from William Contreras, the Brewers got the best of it to secure a 7-4 win and a 2-0 lead in the series.The 11 combined runs were the most scored in an NL playoff game this postseason.The Brewers now stand two wins away from avenging last season's NLCS sweep at the hands of the Dodgers and securing a trip to the World Series.William Contreras helped spark the Brewers to a 2-0 NLCS lead.Aaron Gash via Getty ImagesWith All-Star and reigning World Series MVP Yoshinobu Yamamoto on the mound for the Dodgers and standout rookie Logan Henderson starting for the Brewers, Game 2 was projected to resemble Milwaukee's 2-1 win in Game 1.Instead, each starter labored through 39 pitches in the first two innings, and the Dodgers took a 2-1 lead into the bottom of the third. Then the Brewers ended Yamamoto's day.Yamamoto comes back down to Earth Yamamoto issued two walks in the third, including a two-out free pass to Jake Bauers after a 12-pitch battle that loaded the bases. Then captain Christian Yelich delivered with a two-run single to give Milwaukee a 3-2 lead.CHRISTIAN YELICH COMES THROUGH!BREWERS LEAD pic.twitter.com/eZ2VMwaYki— MLB (@MLB) October 12, 2026 With that, Yamamoto's day was done. Milwaukee forced him to throw 36 pitches in the third inning, in which he recorded just two outs, and Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made the call to his bullpen. After entering Monday's game with a 1.07 ERA over his five previous playoff starts, Yamomoto allowed 3 earned runs on 4 hits and 2 walks in 2 2/3 innings. He recorded just 1 strikeout.The Dodgers weren't finished, though. Defensive mistakes from the Brewers, including two throwing errors by Henderson, allowed them to retake the lead at 4-3. They chased Henderson after two batters reached with no outs in the fifth.Contreras delivers with multiple clutch hitsContreras answered back in the bottom of the fifth with a solo home run to tie the game 4-4.WILD BILL GOES OFF THE SCOREBOARD pic.twitter.com/tLgKSYREhX— Milwaukee Brewers (@Brewers) October 12, 2026 Contreras then delivered again with an RBI single in the sixth to spot Milwaukee a 5-4 lead. The Brewers never trailed again.William Contreras puts the Brewers in front!He's got 3 RBI tonight 💪 pic.twitter.com/IHA682RpfR— MLB (@MLB) October 12, 2026 Contreras also knocked in the first Brewers run in the first inning. He finished his day 3-for-4 at the plate with 1 walk, 1 home run, 1 run scored and 3 RBI.Brewers bullpen makes historyWhile eight Dodgers pitchers failed to contain the Brewers' bats, Milwaukee's bullpen finished the game with five perfect frames.After Henderson was pulled with no outs in the fifth, Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby combined to secure the final 15 outs of the game without allowing a baserunner. Per the Fox broadcast, that's the first time in playoff history that a bullpen has pitched five or more innings without allowing a baserunner to end a game.Ohtani, Dodgers stars struggle at the plateThe vaunted top of the Dodgers order of Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Shohei Ohtani combined to go 1-for-13 with 1 walk in Game 2. Betts accounted for the hit and the walk.Ohtani, who's still reeling from nagging injuries, finished 0-for-4 with 2 strikeouts. He's now 1-for-7 in this series and is slashing.150/.261/.150 in the postseason.JoJo Romero strikes out Shohei Ohtani, who had a hard time holding onto the bat pic.twitter.com/oYILwD38cj— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 12, 2026 The Dodgers will need more production from their stars and a better outing from projected starter Blake Snell in Game 3 on Wednesday (8 p.m. ET), or they'll risk falling into an 0-3 hole in the series.

images.caption: William Contreras helped spark the Brewers to a 2-0 NLCS lead. (Aaron Gash via Getty Images)

articles.title: Guardians rally to stun Rays with late-game onslaught, steal ALCS Game 1 on the road
articles.summary: This time last week, the Cleveland Guardians were in an 0-2 hole and in danger of being swept by the White Sox in the ALDS. Now they're three wins away from the World Series.
articles.body: This time last week, the Cleveland Guardians were in an 0-2 hole and in danger of being swept by the Chicago White Sox in the ALDS.Now they're three wins away from playing in the World Series. The Guardians rallied from a 2-0 deficit in Game 1 of the American League Championship Series to secure a 7-3 win over the favored Tampa Bay Rays on Monday. With the win, the Guardians have stolen home-field advantage as the series begins in Tampa.Tampa Bay, which had not trailed in the postseason until Monday, struck early against Guardians starter Foster Griffin with two runs on four hits in the first inning as eight Rays batters went to the plate. It looked like more of the same from a Rays team that finished the regular season with five more wins than any other team in the American League.José Ramírez and Chase DeLauter both had big nights to lead the Guardians past the Rays in Game 1.Julio Aguilar via Getty ImagesGuardians finally crack Drew Rasmussen with 2 homersEarly on, Rays ace Drew Rasmussen was in full control on the heels of his one-hit effort in a shutout of the New York Yankees in Game 1 of the ALDS. He started Monday's game with five scoreless innings to extend his postseason shutout streak to 13 consecutive frames.But a pair of first-pitch home runs ended that streak.Chase DeLauter delivered with a towering, opposite-field shot on Rasmussen's first pitch of the sixth, which cut Tampa Bay's lead in half.Chase DeLauter gets a run back for the Guardians! pic.twitter.com/dtYgH6QdbB— MLB (@MLB) October 13, 2026 Then, with Rasmussen at 90 pitches, Rays manager Kevin Cash opted to send his ace back out for the seventh. It's a decision that backfired immediately.Patrick Bailey tied the game with another solo home run, this one off Rasmussen's first pitch of the inning.Patrick Bailey ties the game with a solo shot! pic.twitter.com/U8nPaiucVO— MLB (@MLB) October 13, 2026 With that, the game was tied, and Rasmussen's night was done. Guardians do damage after Rasmussen's exitFrom there, the Guardians continued to rally against Tampa Bay's bullpen.In the top of the eighth, a José Ramírez single and DeLauter double put runners on second and third with no outs. A Nathaniel Lowe liner to center field sent them both home for a 4-2 lead, and the Guardians never trailed again.Lowe for the lead!Cleveland #Guardians (1B) Nathaniel Lowe drives in a pair of runs in the 8th inning vs the Rays.#StandGuard pic.twitter.com/5zbvyBTTzH— Guardians Prospective (@CleGuardPro) October 13, 2026 Tampa Bay responded with a solo home run from Cedric Mullins in the bottom of the eighth. But the Guardians piled on in the top of the ninth, stifling any hope of a Tampa Bay comeback. Ramírez extended the lead to 5-3 with a two-out RBI single. Then he and DeLauter came home courtesy of a two-run Jo Adell double down the left-field line after DeLauter drew a six-pitch walk.Welcome to the Jo Show.#GuardsBall | #StandGuard pic.twitter.com/EKoXiCJpuy— Cleveland Guardians (@CleGuardians) October 13, 2026 The clutch hit extended Cleveland's lead to the final 7-3 margin and capped a big night for both Ramírez and DeLauter.Guardians' stars show outOn Monday, Ramírez went 3-for-5 at the plate with two runs scored and an RBI. DeLauter finished a triple short of the cycle while going 3-for-4 with a home run, an RBI and three runs scored. The pair accounted for six of Cleveland's 14 hits as eight Guardians batters recorded hits against Tampa Bay pitching. The effort continued an offensive outburst from the previous series, as the Guardians scored nine runs in consecutive ALDS wins against the White Sox before closing out the series with a 2-0 win in Game 5.Six Cleveland pitchers, meanwhile, limited the Rays to just one run after Griffin's two-run first.The Rays will look to midseason acquisition Freddy Peralta (4.42 ERA, 1.325 WHIP in regular season) to turn things around on the mound in Game 2 on Tuesday. The Guardians are scheduled to counter with All-Star Parker Messick (2.56 ERA, 1.063 WHIP).

articles.title: A rare and shocking stinker from Yoshinobu Yamamoto, combined with another no-show from the offense, puts Dodgers into 0-2 hole in NLCS vs. Brewers
articles.summary: Yamamoto threw just 2 2/3 innings in Game 2, marking the shortest outing of his postseason career.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — Yoshinobu Yamamoto wasn't sure, couldn't say, didn't yet understand.

It must have been a foreign feeling for the Dodgers' ace, a successful man obsessed with details and generally unaccustomed to failure. Yamamoto had just delivered the single worst outing of his spectacular, historic postseason career. He went just 2 2/3 innings against the Milwaukee Brewers in Los Angeles' NLCS Game 2 loss on Monday . It was his shortest October start ever.

And so Yamamoto sat beside interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda atop the postgame podium and tried to answer questions about an afternoon gone wrong. He wore a blue Dodgers hoodie and an expression of bewilderment.

"I don't know the exact reason yet," the 2025 World Series MVP admitted via Sonoda. "I need to check the videos, and then I can reflect on what happened today."

He'll have ample time to contemplate his outing on a long, quiet flight home to Los Angeles. And if the Dodgers don't win two ballgames this week at Chavez Ravine, Yamamoto might spend the entire winter dwelling on this one. The prospect of a Game 6 back at American Family Field is no longer a certainty. Because the Los Angeles Dodgers — back-to-back champs and baseball's boogeyman — are reeling, down two games to zero in this best-of-seven set.

"Well, we threw out three hits tonight ... " manager Dave Roberts reflected after his team's disheartening 7-4 defeat . "Some of it was the starter, some of it the bullpen. I don't have an answer why."

This sense of confusion, clearly felt by Roberts, Yamamoto and other members of DodgerLand, is perfectly reasonable. Not since the 2023 NLDS have the Dodgers dropped the first two games of a postseason series. Shohei Ohtani was an Anaheim Angel then. Kyle Tucker was a Houston Astro. Yamamoto was an Orix Buffalo. After that shocking 2023 exit to a less talented Arizona Diamondbacks team, the Dodgers reoriented the balance of sport by adding Ohtani and Yamamoto.

They are 8-0 in postseason series since then.

"It was tough," Mookie Betts said about watching the typically metronomic Yamamoto stumble. "But you know, he's a human being. I think everybody is so used to him being a robot."

Yamamoto took the mound on Monday owning the second-lowest postseason ERA in MLB history among pitchers with at least 10 playoff starts. He strolled off that same hill a little more than an hour later, shellshocked, with just eight outs recorded and three earned runs on his ledger. The setting Wisconsin sun pierced through the open stadium windows. Many in the crowd, smelling blood and feeling hope, waved Yamamoto a tongue-in-cheek goodbye.

Milwaukee's offense deserves a mountain of credit for grinding Yamamoto down. The Brewers' lineup made Game 2 a war of attrition from the jump. Yamamoto needed 25 pitches to finish a rocky first inning marked by a William Contreras RBI single. After a clean second, trouble found Yamamoto in the third.

Elongated plate appearances from David Hamilton (six pitches, single), Brice Turang (six pitches, walk) and Contreras (seven pitches, flyout) put Yamamoto on the ropes. Then an epic, 12-pitch showdown with Jake Bauers that ended with a bases-loading walk squeezed Yamamoto dry. Christian Yelich provided the knockout blow with a go-ahead single to put Milwaukee up 3-2 and end Yamamoto's night.

There were a few borderline calls along the way that went unchallenged by backstop Will Smith. Perhaps a head tap or two might have stopped the bleeding, but there's no challenging how adrift Yamamoto looked. He finished the inning having thrown 36 pitches, the most he has thrown in a single frame all year.

"He just didn't have it tonight, which is very rare," Roberts said.

But even with Yamamoto beaten and bested, the Dodgers still had a chance to win this game. Uncharacteristically sloppy play from the Brewers helped keep the window propped open. Los Angeles' offense scored its first run without the help of a hit, added its second on a wayward pickoff attempt and retook the lead 4-3 in the fifth after Milwaukee starter Logan Henderson hurled a sac bunt past an outstretched Bauers down the left-field line.

That turned out to be the Dodgers' last baserunner. Milwaukee hopped back in front against reliever Brock Stewart in the sixth, then padded the lead in the eighth. Los Angeles' collection of stars had no answer for a dialed-in Brewers bullpen that recorded 15 straight outs to end the game.

The Dodgers' hitters are a group in dire straits.

"They had much better at-bats than we did across the board, top-to-bottom," Roberts lamented afterward.

Ohtani and Smith continued their unfathomably barren postseason, going a combined 0-for-8 in Game 2 to push their combined playoff line to 4-for-43 with zero extra-base hits and 15 strikeouts. Baseball is notoriously random, unpredictable, unforgiving, but this is a shocking cold stretch from two of the game's most accomplished hitters. Smith hit a few balls well on Monday. Ohtani, still compromised physically, did not. He struck out twice, including on a bizarre half-swing in the sixth inning that sent his bat twirling into the air.

"It's hard to see, but he's working, and hopefully he gets out of it," Betts said of Ohtani. "We need him, for sure."

Ohtani, for the sixth consecutive time this postseason, was not made available to the media after Game 2. The last we heard from the four-time MVP was on the workout day ahead of NLDS Game 1. His outlook, at that point, was soaked in optimism.

"[My body] feels really good overall. I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there," Ohtani said on Oct. 2. He's 3-for-20 since then.

The mood was predictably dour in Los Angeles' clubhouse after the loss. Players ate dinner, showered, donned matching dark-gray tracksuits and filed toward the bus.

Sonoda, Yamamoto's interpreter, yet to don his team-brand sweatshirt, bounced across the room in a slightly more conspicuous outfit. He wore a navy blue shirt , featuring a picture of a black pug on a white background just above the word "Bruh."

articles.title: Ex-Toronto Blue Jays Pitcher Officially Becomes Free Agent Amid MLB Playoffs
articles.summary: A former Toronto Blue Jays pitcher officially became a free agent on Monday amid the American and National League Championship Series. The post Ex-Toronto Bl...
articles.body:
Unfortunately, the Toronto Blue Jays are watching the MLB playoffs from home.

Just four teams remain in the postseason. The Cleveland Guardians are playing the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALCS. The Los Angeles Dodgers are playing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS.

On Monday, the Brewers took a 2-0 lead in the NLCS with a Game 2 win. The Guardians took a 1-0 lead with a Game 1 victory.

Also on Monday, a former Blue Jays pitcher officially became an MLB free agent.

Former Blue Jays RHP Derek Law Officially Becomes Free Agent

Former Blue Jays right-hander Derek Law elected free agency on Monday, according to MiLB.com's transactions log .

Law, 36, pitched for the Blue Jays in 2019.

In his lone season with Toronto, Law posted a 4.90 ERA with a 1.67 WHIP and 67 strikeouts over 60 2/3 innings.

Law spent this past season in the Arizona Diamondbacks organization.

The right-hander allowed one run in nine innings across seven outings with Arizona this year. He spent most of the season in Triple-A.

The San Francisco Giants selected Law in the ninth round of the 2011 MLB Draft out of Miami Dade College, Kendall Campus.

Law made his MLB debut with San Francisco in 2016.

The right-hander pitched for the Giants through the 2018 season before joining the Blue Jays in 2019.

Law didn't make a single MLB appearance in 2020. Since then, he has logged innings for the Minnesota Twins , Detroit Tigers, Cincinnati Reds, Washington Nationals and Diamondbacks. He didn't pitch in the majors last year before throwing for Arizona this season.

articles.title: Early 2026-27 MLB Offseason Predictions on Free Agency, Trades and More
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB season is over for all but four teams, which is how you know the offseason is getting closer every day. And it could be a big one.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB season is over for all but four teams, which is how you know the offseason is getting closer every day. And it could be a big one.

Yes, we all know there's likely a lockout coming at the start of December. And no, this year's class of free agents is not particularly strong. Yet one can still imagine a whole bunch of big moves going down, so what's the harm in making predictions?

We have come to present 10 for the 2026-27 offseason. They touch on six potential free agents and four potential trade targets. Each is a big swing in its own way.

Let's begin in San Diego, with a move that won't be happening.

The San Diego Padres Won't Let Michael King Reach Free Agency

Michael King can opt out of the last two years of his three-year, $75 million contract, and he'd be a fool not to after the year he just had.

The 3.21 ERA and 185.0 innings he posted for his 32 starts in the regular season? Pretty good. The one run he allowed in 14.0 innings during the Padres' playoff run? Even better.

Yet despite his ties to the East Coast, King made no bones about his desire to carry on with the Padres: "San Diego's been—been incredible for me, and it's all the way across the country from home. But now I feel like I have a—a second home on the West Coast, so it's been awesome. And yeah, I hope to—hope to continue."

That reads like an invitation to the Padres to make an offer, and they darn well should. Their rotation simply can't afford to lose King. And if Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano want to throw one of MLB's most loyal fanbases a bone in their first winter as the team's owners, they'd do well to pony up for King.

We'll go out on a limb and guess that they won't even let the 31-year-old righty reach the open market, a la the Kansas City Royals with Michael Wacha two years ago . The final contract should be in the nine-figure range.

The Philadelphia Phillies Will Trade for Jarren Duran

Shifting now to the trade market, there might not be a more obvious offseason trade candidate than Jarren Duran.

He's just not the central figure in Boston that he was in 2024, when he was the All-Star Game MVP en route to a 9.0-rWAR season. His production especially cratered this year, in which even 21 home runs could not save him from an output of 0.4 rWAR.

The 30-year-old is also a spare part for the Red Sox, as he's one of three left-handed-hitting outfielders for two spots on either side of Ceddanne Rafaela. He'd fit better on the Phillies, who got -0.2 rWAR from left field this season.

It would also be a reunion of sorts. Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski was still running the Red Sox when they drafted Duran in 2018. Despite his recent slide, he's still proven to be one of the top players from that year's draft class.

As for what a deal could look like, how does everyone like the sound of this challenge trade? Duran for Orion Kerkering.

The Chicago Cubs Will Trade for George Kirby

It's a rare thing, to have enough starting pitching to be able to even think about trading away an All-Star starter.

That is precisely the position the Mariners are in, and one can imagine them trading Logan Gilbert, George Kirby or Bryan Woo if the price was right. We're zeroing in on Kirby just because it's easiest to imagine him going somewhere.

He's in a sweet spot: He's lost some stock as an ace but remains appealing on account of his excellent stuff, strong command and combination of youth (28) and controllability (through 2028). If the Mariners can turn him into a controllable bat, they should.

Given their previous interest in Kirby, this is where the Cubs could come in. They stand to lose basically an entire rotation's worth of starters to free agency, including Kevin Gausman, Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga. They should look to re-sign some guys, but bringing in fresh blood via trade is likewise a good idea.

A Kirby-for-Matt Shaw trade works on paper, even if it would require the Cubs to backfill Shaw's spot. To that end, re-signing Ian Happ and/or Seiya Suzuki would do the trick.

The Tampa Bay Rays Will Trade for Hunter Goodman

We'll see how the Rays do in the ALCS against the Cleveland Guardians, but dare we say they should be plotting a big offseason either way?

There is, after all, a bit of a power vacuum in the AL East. The Toronto Blue Jays and Baltimore Orioles are on the fritz. The New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox both figure to be active this winter, yet neither club looms as large over the division as they did in the 2000s and 2010s.

Meanwhile, the Rays are hoping to have their new stadium ready for the 2029 season. The thing to do in the meantime is build the hype, and then deliver a team that represents a newer, better era of Rays baseball.

A trade for Hunter Goodman would do the trick. He had more home runs this year (41) than the Rays have gotten from the catching position across the last three years (36). Conveniently, the 27-year-old is controlled through 2029.

The Rays were linked to Goodman at the trade deadline, and they're one of relatively few teams with enough prospect depth to overwhelm the Colorado Rockies. Any offer headlined by Grady Emerson or Theo Gillen could get it done.

The Atlanta Braves Will Trade for Gunnar Henderson

We did say big swings, right? And truth be told, there may not be a better time than this winter for the Baltimore Orioles to trade Gunnar Henderson.

Similar to Jarren Duran and George Kirby, he's another guy whose stock has gone in the wrong direction in recent years. His 65 homers and 14.9 rWAR made him a superstar in 2023 and 2024. Across 2025 and 2026, those totals fell to 41 homers and 8.6 rWAR.

The free-agent market is so barren, however, that other teams might just be willing to pay the Orioles' price for Henderson rather than the price he's actually worth. He'd indeed be a worthwhile project, given that he's still just 25 years old and controlled through 2028.

If the Braves don't already have Henderson on their radar, they should. Their shortstop position has been unsettled for years, and it stands to be wide-open once Ha-Seong Kim and Mauricio Dubón file for free agency.

According to Peter Abraham of The Boston Globe , the Braves weren't willing to move Didier Fuentes in a rental trade for Tarik Skubal. Would they reconsider if it meant getting Henderson for at least two years?

The Los Angeles Angels Will Sign Jazz Chisholm Jr.

Following their sweep at the hands of the Rays in the ALDS, Jazz Chisholm Jr. came right out and said it : "This is where I want to be. I love it as a Yankee."

Unlike with Michael King and the Padres, however, this doesn't feel like a situation where the love will be mutual. The Yankees have seemed ready to move on from Chisholm for months, and they have two potential replacements at second base in Anthony Volpe and Luis García Jr.

Chisholm could be in for a multi-year deal. Yet after falling well short of his 50-50 goal and posting just 1.7 rWAR this year, the 28-year-old might be better off pursuing a one-year contract and reentering the market next winter.

The Angels are just one of many teams that would have to be interested in such a deal. They are in need of help at the keystone, specifically, and upside on offense, generally. Chisholm can provide both, and some energy to boot.

Depending on when the sale is finalized, signing Chisholm would also be a relatively low-risk way for Stan Kroenke to ingratiate himself with his new fanbase. Even if a one-year deal for Chisholm is valued at $20-plus million, he can afford it.

The Toronto Blue Jays Will Sign Seiya Suzuki

Let's cut right to the chase, because Mitch Bannon of The Athletic didn't leave much doubt about where the Blue Jays stand on Seiya Suzuki:

"This offseason, said a league source who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss offseason plans, the Jays are expected to pursue Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki."

The Blue Jays need a right fielder. More than that, they just plain need reliable hitters after finishing last in MLB in scoring this year. Suzuki more than makes the grade, as his last four seasons have seen him average a 131 OPS+ and 25 home runs.

Suzuki might be able to top the $85 million guarantee that landed him with the Chicago Cubs back in 2022. Too much for other teams, perhaps. It shouldn't be for these Blue Jays, who have been plenty willing to spend in recent offseasons.

The New York Yankees Will Sign Teruaki Sato

Should the Yankees pivot away from their power-based offense and toward something more holistic? Probably.

But will they actually do it? One thinks not, and not just because "Bronx Bombers" is their whole brand. When you have a home park that caters to power as much as Yankee Stadium, you don't waste that advantage. Least of all when you can afford power like the Yankees can.

Given this and their need to upgrade at least one corner of the infield, it came as no surprise when Jon Heyman of the New York Post tabbed the Yankees as a fit for Teruaki Sato in August.

The 27-year-old's profile bears a resemblance to that of Munetaka Murakami. There's a lot of swing-and-miss, and he's probably more of a first baseman than a third baseman. But he's also hit 79 home runs across the last two seasons in Japan. That's as a left-handed hitter, making him a classic candidate to take aim at Yankee Stadium's short porch.

Murakami didn't land a nine-figure deal last winter, and we all saw how that worked out for everyone who sold him short as an impact player. Sato may benefit from a market correction, especially if the Yankees get involved.

The Boston Red Sox Will Sign Randy Arozarena

If anything is a sure bet for the coming offseason, it's that Randy Arozarena will end up back on the East Coast.

It's where he became a star with the Rays, and Ryan Divish of The Seattle Times claims Arozarena was "crushed" when he got traded to the Pacific Northwest in 2024. Lucky for him, he's headed to free agency at a moment when several East Coast teams need a potent right-handed bat.

The Red Sox are one of them, and they indeed need more power in general. They have ranked in the bottom half of the AL in home runs in four of the last five seasons. Of the three players who topped 20 homers for them this year, one (Jarren Duran) is a candidate to move this winter.

True, it's harder to count on the Red Sox to spend money in free agency than it used to be. Yet the capacity to spend is still there, and one would hope the willingness is too after back-to-back playoff humiliations at the hands of the Yankees.

To this point in his career, Arozarena has been a steady 20-20 threat. If the Red Sox spend $100-plus million to put him in Fenway Park, his potential in the home run column should inch closer to 30.

The New York Mets Will Sign Tarik Skubal

The Mets have a good shot at Tarik Skubal simply by virtue of being one of very few teams that can afford him.

When ESPN's Kiley McDaniel solicited projections for the two-time Cy Young Award winner's next contract, the average came out to eight years, $355 million. It would be the fourth-largest contract in the history of MLB free agency, and the largest for a full-time pitcher.

At that rate, the Skubal sweepstakes could come down to which of the Mets, Dodgers or Yankees would be most willing to take the risk. And of those three clubs, the Mets may have the clearest need for a No. 1 starter this winter.

Whether David Stearns would want to shell out so much money for Skubal is a fair question, but what he wants might not matter if Steve Cohen decides to step in. He notably did so to land Juan Soto on a 15-year, $765 million deal.

Soto's agent? Scott Boras. Skubal's agent? Also Boras. Suffice it to say he'll know who to call if he smells green in Queens.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Dodgers will have 'conversation' about benching Shohei Ohtani as star's struggles continue this postseason
articles.summary: The Dodgers are considering the unthinkable down 0-2 to the Brewers.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are getting desperate down 0-2 in the National League Championship Series. With their backs against the wall, the team will reportedly have a "conversation" with two-way star Shohei Ohtani about sitting him in Game 3, per The Athletic.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts didn't explicitly confirm he would bench Ohtani in Game 3, but said he would have a "conversation" with the superstar after Ohtani took some horrid at-bats in Game 2, per The Athletic.

"Yeah, I mean, obviously it hasn't been good. He doesn't feel great. I think for me, it's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it. "I'll have [that conversation] with him tomorrow."

"Yeah, I mean, obviously it hasn't been good. He doesn't feel great. I think for me, it's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it.

"I'll have [that conversation] with him tomorrow."

Ohtani has had a rough start to the series, going 1-for-7 with three strikeouts against the Milwaukee Brewers. While that would normally be written off as a small-sample slump, Ohtani has been subject to criticism over taking non-competitive at-bats. His strikeout against JoJo Romero in the sixth inning of Game 2, in particular, led some to worry that Ohtani might be too compromised to keep playing in the series.

That wasn't Ohtani's only concerning at-bat during the series. He's been consistently beat by velocity and reportedly tried to shorten his swing to try and go the other way with pitches, per The Athletic.

His struggles haven't been limited to the NLCS, either. This postseason, Ohtani is just 3 of 20, with three walks and seven strikeouts. His three hits have been singles, giving him a .150/.261/.150 slash line over six games.

Perhaps most concerning, however, is the fact that Ohtani hasn't been himself for quite some time now. Since Aug. 14, Ohtani hit .198/.305/.363 over his final 23 games of the regular season. He was placed on the injured list in the middle of that stretch due to knee and biceps injuries.

While Ohtani was given a break to recover from both issues, he returned to action still dealing with the ailments. Ahead of the team's National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves, Ohtani admitted he would have to "manage" both injuries during the playoffs.

Thus far, Ohtani hasn't been able to manage the injuries effectively enough. The Dodgers seemed to recognize that much early in the postseason, dropping Ohtani in the batting order .

That hasn't been enough, forcing the Dodgers into a tough situation ahead of Game 3 on Wednesday. Los Angeles has the talent to excel even if Ohtani needs to miss time. Whether the team is brave enough to make that decision could be the difference between coming back in the NLCS or watching the World Series at home.

articles.title: Doncaster councillor sanctioned over offensive Facebook posts
articles.summary: Sub-committee members recommend that Carl Miller be removed from all council appointments.
articles.body:
A town councillor has been sanctioned after comments he posted on Facebook were found to be "derogatory or offensive".

Carl Miller, who sits on Hatfield Town Council, in Doncaster, suggested renaming the town with a racial slur and said it was being "overwhelmed" by migrants in a post shared on 19 April.

He said at a hearing on Friday that the names he suggested were "real places" elsewhere in the world.

However, a sub-committee found the posts had breached the councillors' code of conduct.

Miller began his post by saying: "Having spent all day in my front garden, I could somehow be forgiven for thinking that my house has been moved to Africa," the Local Democracy Reporting Service said .

He then made reference to the "Great Replacement" - a conspiracy theory which alleges that populations of white Europeans are being replaced by non-white people.

Miller, who does not represent a political party on the council, also posted a complaint about Labour MP Lee Pitcher, in which he repeated a racial slur and complained that family homes were being given to migrants.

The two posts were investigated after a complaint by Reform UK councillor Isaiah-John Smith-Reasbeck.

Sub-committee members recommended that Miller be removed from all council appointments.

At the same hearing, Miller was also disciplined for suggesting that fellow Hatfield town councillor Linda Curran would arrive at meetings "drunk".

Councillor Michael Glynn was also reprimanded for suggesting Curran "appeared to me to be a little bit worse for the wear for drinking" at council meetings.

Curran said she had never attended meetings drunk and that the claim from Miller was "defamatory".

Speaking after the hearing, she said: "I would like to thank the officers, Neil Concannon and his team, for their investigation of my complaint.

"Also, the audit committee for their time in listening to my complaints."

She added: "I believe people should be able to disagree in politics without it becoming a personal attack and abusive."

The sub-committee issued five sanctions against Miller and Glynn, including a requirement to issue a written apology to Curran and undertake training.

articles.summary: The MLB offseason is very much on for 26 of the league's 30 teams.
articles.body:
The MLB offseason is very much on for 26 of the league's 30 teams.

It has been for quite a while now for the non-playoff participants.

While this offseason carries less certainty than most (with looming CBA negotiations pointing toward a likely lockout), it should have the same intrigue as always. There are, after all, a number of interesting free agents on the market, including perhaps the best pitcher on the planet.

So, while before the Championship Series get going again, let's dive into the latest free-agency buzz and use it to shape some predictions for the players involved.

Had free agency came one year earlier for Jazz Chisholm Jr., he might have been fielding blank-check offers. In 2025, he appeared as one of the most dynamic hitters in the sport, garnering both All-Star and Silver Slugger honors while tallying 31 homers and 31 stolen bases.

But he wasn't a free agent then. He is now, and his stock isn't nearly as high after struggling with consistency and managing just 19 homers this time around. Even worse, this market seems rich with second-base alternatives, as Chisholm will be joined on the open market by Brandon Lowe, Luis Arraez, Gleyber Torres and Mauricio Dubón.

For these reasons and more, Chisholm's tenure with the New York Yankees could be finished. As MLB.com's Mark Feinsand relayed, "it feels like the Yankees are ready to move on with one of their other options at second base."

It's not all doom and gloom for Chisholm, though. His talent can still appear electric, and he's only 28 years old. He'll have interest from other teams, and he should still command a good deal of respect—even if it's not what it would have been last winter.

Prediction: Chisholm signs with the Los Angeles Angels.

Padres To Factor in Tarik Skubal Sweepstakes?

The list of teams likely to have interest in two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal might go 30-teams deep. The list of clubs who can actually afford the 29-year-old potential record-setter is a lot smaller.

While so much of that process still needs to play out, it's already fair to wonder whether this might be a two-team race between the deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets. It could absolutely play out that way, but that's not a reflection of the current market.

ESPN's Kiley McDaniel recently surveyed a batch of league insiders about Skubal's free agency, and the San Diego Padres were brought up as sleeper suitors. Moreover, they "seemed to be the consensus pick for the most serious bidder" in the sleeper group, which also included the Los Angeles Angels and Chicago White Sox.

The Padres won 91 games and a playoff series this season, but they had trouble generating quality from their injury-riddled rotation outside of ace Michael King (who's also a free agent). The need for San Diego is obvious. It still might be enough to convince the Padres to fork over the kind of cash needed to get a deal done.

Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Brandon Lowe Priced Himself Out of Pittsburgh?

Give the Pittsburgh Pirates a chance to redo their 2025 offseason trade for Brandon Lowe, and they wouldn't change a thing. Well, other than maybe the contract he brought with him.

He arrived with a single season left on his deal and promptly delivered the kind of contract-year campaign impending free agents all dream about. He belted 35 homers, tallied 190 combined runs and RBI and posted a career-best 5.4 wins above replacement .

He was, frankly, perhaps too good for Pittsburgh, since it might balk at the contract terms likely needed to bring him back.

"He'll hit the open market as one of the most highly coveted position players available," MLB.com's Aiden Stepansky wrote. "(Pirates general manager Ben) Cherington described the return of Lowe as a 'great outcome if he's a Pirate next year.' But it will cost a pretty penny, likely a sizable increase from the $11.5 million he earned in 2026, and Lowe, at 32 years old, could find interest in a longer-term deal."

Maybe the Pirates' 82 wins, their most since 2018, will embolden them to spend, though Lowe's contract could feature both a big annual salary and a good amount of years. That combination might be more than Pittsburgh's front office can stomach, which would be music to the ears of a certain major-market big-spender with question marks at Lowe's second base position.

Prediction: Lowe signs with the New York Yankees.

articles.title: MLB insider fears Dodgers are out of time to make an NLCS comeback down 0-2
articles.summary: This insider doesn't believe the Dodgers can come back from down 0-2 in the NLCS.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers made it to the NLCS amid their pursuit of their third straight World Series title. Facing the Milwaukee Brewers , the Dodgers have shown life through two games, but they're down 0-2 in the series so far.

With the series shifting to Los Angeles for the next three games, can the Dodgers make a comeback and reach the World Series? It's entirely possible, especially if they can get after the Brewers' pitching more going forward.

However, MLB insider Ken Rosenthal for The Athletic believes that this is the end for the Dodgers. He doesn't believe Los Angeles can make this comeback, as it's "difficult to imagine" this Dodgers team winning four of the next five games in this NLCS.

MLB insider believes Dodgers' season might be over down 0-2 to Brewers

"It's not over. But if you were to picture the end of the Los Angeles Dodgers' championship run, this is how it would look, no?" Rosenthal writes.

What Rosenthal is referring to is the injury and struggles of Shohei Ohtani at the plate; taking away the Dodgers' best player due to an injury certainly hurts their chances of making a run this season.

Add in that the rest of the lineup is continuing to struggle, with one extra-base hit through two games in the NLCS against the Brewers.

Finally, and maybe the most damning, is that "Co-aces Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto lasted a combined 7 2/3 innings in their two starts."

If the Dodgers' best pitchers cannot go deep into these NLCS games, it's going to be incredibly difficult to beat this Brewers team.

Rosenthal wrote that, "It's difficult to imagine the Dodgers taking four of the next five games, even with the next three at home."

He isn't completely writing the Dodgers off just yet, as they're still the Dodgers, and it's "difficult to imagine them just fading away."

While things aren't going well for the Dodgers right now, there is too much talent on this team for them not to make a legitimate push, at least during their three-game homestand.

The Dodgers may rediscover their offense at home and stay alive in this series to at least get it back to Milwaukee for Game 6 or maybe even a Game 7.

But down 0-2 to the Brewers, Rosenthal does believe, to a certain degree, that Los Angeles' chances of winning this series are over. It's not done yet, but Ohtani's issues, the lackluster offense, and the pitching staff's poor play have the Dodgers on the ropes.

articles.title: A Dodgers-less World Series would hurt now, but help MLB later | Bobby Burack
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are now World Series betting favorites over the Los Angeles Dodgers after taking a commanding 2-0 lead in the NLCS.
articles.body: For the first time this season, the Los Angeles Dodgers are not the betting favorites to win the World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers, who lead the Dodgers 2-0 in the NLCS, are the betting favorites to win the World Series. Despite the funeral arrangements demoralized Dodgers are making, Los Angeles isn't eliminated yet. The Blue Jays overcame a 2-0 deficit in the ALCS to defeat the Mariners just last season. Fifteen other teams have done the same. Those aren't great odds, but as Dodgers fans kept reminding everyone while assembling their superteam, baseball is inherently random. Teams get hot. Players go cold. Great lineups disappear for a week. Struggling pitchers suddenly look formidable. We are not writing off this Dodgers team until someone actually eliminates it. Even so, the prospect of a Dodgers-less World Series feels real for the first time in a while. DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS That said, the prospect of a Dodgers-less World Series feels real for the first time in a while. In the short term, a Brewers-Rays/Guardians World Series would hardly be MLB's dream matchup. As pure a form of baseball as those clubs play, they are small-market teams without much national appeal. For comparison, the past two World Series featuring the Dodgers, against the Yankees in 2024 and Blue Jays in 2025, averaged around 15.3 million viewers. In 2023, the Texas Rangers-Arizona Diamondbacks World Series averaged just 9 million. A Brewers-Rays/Guardians matchup would probably land much closer to the 2023 number, barring a long, dramatic seven-game series. However, the long-term gains off the Dodgers missing the World Series could prove worth the smaller viewership this season. The Dodgers have been World Series favorites for nearly the entirety of the past three years, dating back to the signing of Shohei Ohtani in December 2023. There was a brief stretch during Game 7 of last year's World Series when the Dodgers were trailing and the Toronto Blue Jays had shorter live odds. Los Angeles ultimately came back to win, clinching its second straight championship. The Dodgers entered 2026 as even heavier favorites than the past two years after adding Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in the offseason. Then, in August, they traded for Tarik Skubal, arguably the best pitcher in baseball. ESPN MLB insider Jeff Passan likened the 2026 Dodgers to the Avengers, citing their unprecedented collection of star power. The back-to-back champions adding more stars while much of the league declines to spend or trade aggressively has intensified discussion about a potential lockout and demands for a salary cap. Various outlets — including this one and this author — have argued that the growing disparity between the Dodgers and much of MLB is "ruining baseball." To be clear, the Dodgers are not at fault for relentlessly trying to improve. They are doing exactly what every fan should want their team to do. The criticism is directed at a system that allows such a competitive imbalance to develop in the first place. Or, at least, the perception of one. As the NFL has demonstrated, fans need to believe their team has a chance. It doesn't even have to be true. The same handful of franchises tend to contend for the Super Bowl every year. But constant roster turnover gives most fanbases enough reason to talk themselves into hope before each season. Jets and Dolphins fans are, of course, excluded from this demonstration. That becomes harder in baseball when fans suspect their franchise is more likely to trade its homegrown stars to the Dodgers than build around them. The Detroit Tigers' handling of Skubal is an example of that. There's a reason spoiling movies is considered so obnoxious. People don't want to know the ending before the story begins. If the Dodgers erase a 2-0 deficit, advance to the World Series and win a third consecutive championship — still the second-most likely outcome of the postseason, according to sportsbooks — MLB will have an increasingly difficult time convincing fans that the rest of the league isn't playing for second place. It will also become harder to argue that stricter payroll rules aren't necessary. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Technically, MLB's scriptwriters would prefer the Dodgers to come back, reach the World Series, and then dramatically lose Game 7. That would deliver the television audience in the short term without reinforcing the idea that baseball's richest superteam is inevitable in the long term. Still, if we're talking strictly about the long-term health of the sport, the small-market Brewers knocking off perhaps the greatest baseball team ever assembled on paper would suffice.

articles.title: Major League Baseball is experimenting with new rules this fall to fundamentally change the sport
articles.summary: Beyond the infield shift ban, MLB is now testing outfield positioning rules in the Arizona Fall League to combat plunging fly ball batting averages.
articles.body: Beyond the ill-informed effort to demand an unnecessary salary cap in baseball, one of the primary points of discussion around the sport have been the decline in offensive production. Strikeouts continue to increase, while league-wide batting averages have declined. There's an endless discussion around the importance of situational hitting, of putting the ball in play, and the supposed lack of talent among modern hitters. This "back in my day" thinking is wrong for any number of reasons, including the mountain of data we now have demonstrating it, but it ignores several key factors that have impacted the on-field product. Major League Baseball, though, realizes that the reduced run scoring environment doesn't always make for the most exciting viewing. And they're right. DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS One of their initial efforts to combat the surge in run prevention was to restrict infield shifting. For years, infielders were allowed to stand virtually anywhere, including in some extreme cases, in the middle of the outfield. Those shifts significantly reduced the likelihood of ground balls to the pull side turning into hits, as they had for most of baseball history. The league issued some specific guidelines about extreme positioning, essentially requiring shortstops and second basemen to remain on their side of second base, among other changes. Mostly, it worked. League-wide, batting averages on ground balls surged after baseball instituted new rules. Here's how it's looked since 2018: While still low, the mid-.240's represents a significant increase from the shift era. Fans though, might not have noticed more ground ball hits, and the data bears that out. For example, in 2018, there were nearly 54,000 at-bats that ended with a ground ball. In 2026, there were just over 51,000, but a similar number of hits. Ground ball batting average is up, but total overall hits haven't changed. Why would that be? More fly balls. Which is exactly what the league is hoping to address with its potential changes. Thanks to years of data analysis, baseball front offices know that the greatest likelihood of positive outcomes comes from hitting the ball in the air. Theoretically. The best hitters in the league hit the ball hard, and hit in the air. Thanks to the advent of pitch metrics, pitch shaping, and the endless parade of 100mph relievers, hitting in general has gotten harder than ever. Front offices then, have prioritized finding players who might not make contact as frequently, but generate high-quality contact when they do. The data bears that out; outcomes on fly balls and line drives are significantly better than grounders. In 2018, for example, the league hit .402 with a .770 slugging percentage when hitting the ball in the air, compared to .236 with a .258 slugging percentage on ground balls. Here's the problem though, which is what MLB is hoping to address: thanks to the advent of Statcast and the limitless data now available to teams on hitter propensities, defensive positioning is now so good that teams are dramatically reducing success rates on fly balls and liners. We'll get into the data in a minute, but here's a perfect example of this phenomenon from Monday night's NLCS game between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers. To set the scene, the Dodgers had a rally going against Logan Henderson, putting runners at first and second base with nobody out in the top of the third inning in a 1-1 game. Henderson threw Freddie Freeman an awful 0-1 changeup that wound up right in the perfect hitting zone for a left-handed batter. Freeman crushed it, 106.4 mph with a 22 degree launch angle, straight to the right center field gap. Balls put in play with those characteristics are hits 84% of the time, per the league's Statcast page. For the entirety of baseball history, it was a prototypical double. Instead, right fielder Sal Frelick was positioned perfectly, and ran the ball down without even needing to dive. Instead of a bases-clearing double that scores two runs and sets up a potential big inning, it's a fly ball out. Want to know why offense is down? That right there. Despite their reputation as a "play the game the right way" old-school, "back in my day" team, the Brewers use analytics as much, or more, than any team in baseball. Their front office analyzes every single batted ball from Freddie Freeman against right-handed pitchers throwing exactly the type of pitches Logan Henderson throws, then tells their fielders to set up where he's most likely to hit the ball. What a surprise, they were right. And it might have helped them win game two by preventing a big inning. Sure enough, league-wide, teams have gotten increasingly good at limiting offense on fly balls and line drives thanks to defensive positioning. Here's the batting average and slugging percentage from across baseball since 2018 on balls in the air. It's still significantly better to hit the ball in the air than on the ground, but as the data shows, league-wide batting averages on fly balls has dropped dramatically, a whopping 35 points from the "juiced ball" 2019 season, and roughly 20 points from 2018 or 2021. Both in the left-right direction and, just as importantly, by playing deeper than ever. And MLB might be looking to stop it. FanGraphs reported on the apparent test of new defensive positioning rules being tested in the Arizona Fall League, a typical first stop on the long road to new MLB rules. Per their report, "sources indicated to me that the league’s motivation is to see if further limiting the locations where defenders are allowed to stand will create more base-hit action and have a positive impact on the game’s aesthetics." "Dark green hash marks have been painted on the outfield grass and at points along the arc where the infield dirt meets the outfield grass," the report says. "Defenders have to stand within a certain distance of these hash marks when a pitch is thrown." It continues, "In this alignment, infielders are forced to play 'straight up,' while the corner outfielders are closer to the foul lines, and the center fielder is more shallow compared to where we see big league outfielders normally play nowadays. Above the stands, hanging just beneath the press box and visible from the field, are LED boards that show the players whether they are in compliance with the location restrictions." The pitch clock has been unambiguously good, speeding up game times while increasing the action on the field. articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed that Shohei Ohtani will remain part of the team's lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts confirmed that Shohei Ohtani will remain part of the team's lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers.

Roberts said Tuesday that Ohtani was "very convicted" and "adamant" that he's close and feels good enough to play, according to MLB.com's Sonja Chen .

Roberts previously revealed that he was considering benching the four-time MVP after dealing with health issues during the regular season and struggles at the plate to start the playoffs.

The Dodgers currently trail 2-0 in their series against the Brewers.

Ohtani said through his interpreter that his injury-related symptoms have "subdued" as of late, per MLB Network's Jon Morosi .

"I take full responsibility . . . The symptoms shouldn't be the reason I can't hit," he said, per Morosi.

Ohtani appeared in 135 contests during the regular season, his fewest since joining the Dodgers as a free agent in 2023.

The two-way star initially dealt with left knee inflammation in July, which forced him to stop pitching.

Although Ohtani was able to continue hitting during that time, he was eventually placed on the 15-day injured list due to lingering left knee and right biceps issues on Sept. 11.

He returned before the regular season came to a close, but hit just .238 in five appearances.

Ohtani still hasn't looked like his former self in the playoffs, owning a .150 batting average to go along with a .411 OPS in six postseason contests. In the first two games of the NLCS, he went 1-for-7 with three strikeouts.

As the Dodgers look to avoid a 3-0 series deficit and continue their quest for a third consecutive World Series title, they'll need Ohtani to establish himself as a threat in the middle of their lineup once again.

It's worth noting that the 32-year-old was still productive during the regular season despite his health woes, racking up 26 doubles and 30 home runs to go along with 81 RBI.

articles.title: Dave Roberts says Shohei Ohtani will be in NLCS Game 3 lineup despite hitting slump, lingering injuries
articles.summary: Ohtani is 1-for-7 through two games of the NLCS.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters Tuesday afternoon that Shohei Ohtani will be in the lineup for Game 3 of the NLCS on Wednesday.

Roberts said after his team's loss in Game 2 that they would discuss what is best for Ohtani, as the slugger is just 1-for-7 at the plate through two games of the series.

"Yeah, I mean, obviously, it hasn't been good. He doesn't feel great. I think for me, it's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it. "I'll have [that conversation] with him tomorrow."

"Yeah, I mean, obviously, it hasn't been good. He doesn't feel great. I think for me, it's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it.

"I'll have [that conversation] with him tomorrow."

Ohtani reportedly said that he was "very convicted" and "adamant" that he feels good enough to play, per Sonja Chen .

Following Roberts' announcement, the designated hitter spoke to the media through interpreter Will Ireton. He said, in part, "I take full responsibility. … The symptoms shouldn't be the reason why I can't hit."

Ohtani's problem isn't just the lack of results at the plate, with a small-sample slump and three strikeouts. The bigger issue has been the quality of his at-bats.

So far in the NLCS, Ohtani has drawn criticism for taking non-competitive at-bats. His strikeout against JoJo Romero in the sixth inning of Game 2, in particular, led some to worry that Ohtani might be too compromised to continue playing.

The Athletic reported that Ohtani has tried to shorten his swing to avoid getting beaten by velocity and to drive the ball the other way.

His struggles have not been limited to this series. Ohtani is 3-for-20 with three walks and seven strikeouts in the postseason. He hasn't registered an extra-base hit, as all three of his hits have been singles. Over his six postseason games so far, he is slashing just .150/.261/.150.

The Dodgers slugger missed a big chunk of the final month of the regular season because of knee and biceps injuries. Since Aug. 14, he slashed .198/.305/.363 in his final 23 regular-season games.

Ohtani was added to the IL in September and didn't play from Sept. 9 to Sept. 23. And when he was activated, he was still dealing with issues. He admitted ahead of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves that he would need to " manage " both injuries through the playoffs.

On Tuesday, Ohtani spoke about how his injuries have improved. "The symptoms have subdued a lot, especially when I was on the IL," he said. "As of now, the swing is a daily process of trying different things."

The Dodgers seemed to recognize that much early in the postseason, as they dropped Ohtani in the batting order . He hit fourth in the series opener, then moved to fifth for Game 2.

The NLCS is a best-of-seven series, and the Dodgers are down 0-2 to the Milwaukee Brewers as the series moves to Los Angeles for Game 3 on Wednesday .

articles.title: Shohei Ohtani, Dave Roberts project confidence ahead of NLCS Game 3, even as injuries continue to stymie Dodgers superstar
articles.summary: "The symptoms shouldn't be the reason why I can't hit," Ohtani, who hasn't hit, almost certainly because of the symptoms, insisted.
articles.body:
LOS ANGELES — A rising gust of whispers funneled through the subterranean hallways beneath Dodger Stadium. Each media member, once made aware of the unexpected, passed the news on to the next person they saw. The hum grew into a chatter as reporters filed back into the cramped news conference room.

When Ohtani actually entered the room, followed by members of Dodgers PR and his interpreter, Will Ireton, the din turned to silence in an instant, like the shutting off of a transistor radio.

Rarely does the Dodgers superstar speak to the media. During the regular season, the established routine was for Ohtani to answer eight or so questions after games in which he pitched. After his two-way exploits were halted in early July, he was made available only a handful of times.

However, these are not regular circumstances.

The four-time MVP, following an injury-marred second half, is currently a husk of his best self . In six games this postseason, Ohtani is a disastrous 3-for-20 with zero extra-base hits and seven strikeouts. Through it all, the sport's most famous character has looked discombobulated, wounded, compromised, out of sync. His disappearing act is a massive reason the two-time defending World Series champs find themselves down 0-2 to the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLCS.

Ohtani's elongated schneid, according to a report from The Athletic after Game 2 , sparked consideration among Dodgers brass about sitting Ohtani for Game 3. A day off, perhaps, could provide a morsel of healing for Ohtani's aching body.

But prior to the team's workout on Tuesday, manager Dave Roberts told reporters that Ohtani will indeed be in the lineup for Game 3 on Wednesday.

"I did speak to Sho, had a great conversation," Roberts proclaimed. "He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it. He wants to be in there and help us win a ballgame and win a championship."

Ohtani, always reticent to reveal much, echoed that optimism.

"The symptoms have subdued a lot, especially [compared to] when I was on the IL, spending that time just being able to reduce the symptoms," he explained via Ireton.

Instead of blaming his recent underperformance on lingering injuries or physical ailments, Ohtani directed attention toward his swing mechanics.

"The symptoms shouldn't be the reason why I can't hit," Ohtani, who hasn't hit, almost certainly because of the symptoms, insisted.

That sentiment feels somewhat detached from reality. Ohtani's manager, for instance, had this to say about the superstar's physical condition when asked for a specific medical diagnosis.

"It's everything," Roberts said. "It's the upper body, it's the knee, and he's just not perfect. He's not. But in his words, he's ready to go."

The entire scene was a bizarre, fitting culmination to Ohtani's 2026 injury saga. A lack of clean communication between the player and the team likely exacerbated his various ailments earlier in the year. After his pitching was put on pause, Ohtani remained adamant about trying to return to the mound. The Dodgers, somewhat understandably considering Ohtani's grandeur, let the face of the franchise do what he wanted. In doing so, though, they might have failed to protect Ohtani from himself, from his own physical limitations.

While nobody is sympathetic to the game's richest and most dominant organization, the Dodgers were put in a sticky spot. Ask Shohei to prioritize load management, and you risk ticking off the most important player in baseball history, a man who effectively took a paycut to helm a dynasty. Let Ohtani dictate his own path, and you risk injury. Los Angeles chose door No. 2, and it might damn its season.

Perhaps Ohtani is correct, and he's a few tweaks away from rediscovering the magic. Maybe he reemerges in Game 3, sends Dodger Stadium into pandemonium and leads the club to a three-peat. He has conjured grander miracles.

That's the thing about miracles — they defy the laws of nature. For most of his baseballing life, Ohtani has attempted and succeeded in doing just that. Father Time, however, is undefeated. Age will eventually reduce Ohtani; if not now, then one day in the future.

If he doesn't accept that reality, that moment might come sooner than anybody in Dodger blue wants.

articles.title: Joe Girardi Defends Aaron Boone, Calls Out Jazz Chisholm & Yankees Accountability After Playoff Exit
articles.summary: Former New York Yankees' manager Joe Girardi defended the embattled Aaron Boone during an appearance on The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman, saying he felt Boone did his best managing job yet.
articles.body:
Former New York Yankees' manager Joe Girardi defended the embattled Aaron Boone during an appearance on The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman , saying he felt Boone did his best managing job yet.

"I think you could argue this was his best year of managing," he said on the show . "I think he got the most out of this team during the course of the season with all they had to deal with. And the way they won games, he had to flip the way they won games. They had to win them from a pitching standpoint, different from some of the years past where they would win by just out-slugging people. He couldn't do that this year. And I think he ran the bullpen extremely well and got the most out of those guys."

Instead, Girardi felt the players needed to be more accountable. He in particular referenced Jazz Chisholm Jr. telling reporters after a wild, out-of-control error in Game 2 of the Tampa Bay Rays' ALDS sweep over the Yankees that he would have made the same play again if given the chance, much to the bewilderment of... everyone.

"It's hard to say, because I'm not in the clubhouse every day. But there are things that happen where you wonder, 'Is someone saying anything?' You said you would have done the same thing over again? No! You can't do the same thing! It didn't work!" Girardi said on the The Show (31:00 mark). "Some of the base-running [miscues], all the sliding over bases—someone's got to say something, enough is enough."

There are plenty of fingers to blame for fans as they dissect a 17th straight season without a World Series title. Boone—who has only gotten the team past the ALDS three times since taking over in 2018 and into the World Series just once—and general manager Brian Cashman have been a popular scapegoats. But the players have to own a major stake in 2026's disappointment as well.

articles.title: Freddy Peralta's gem, José Ramírez's blunder lead Rays past Guardians to tie ALCS
articles.summary: After a Game 1 loss, the Rays needed a Game 2 hero to avoid falling into an 0-2 hole at home. Freddy Peralta stepped up.
articles.body: After a Game 1 loss for their first defeat of the postseason, the Tampa Bay Rays needed a Game 2 hero to avoid digging an 0-2 hole at home.Freddy Peralta stepped up.The trade-deadline acquisition from the New York Mets, who has turned a corner since joining the Rays, delivered with six scoreless innings in a sensational start Tuesday. His effort anchored a 3-1 win for Tampa Bay in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series.The win was aided by a blunder from seven-time Guardians All-Star José Ramírez, who's used to playing the hero for Cleveland. But on Tuesday, it was a fourth-inning error by Ramírez that allowed the Rays to take control with three unearned runs.With the victory, the Rays tied the ALCS 1-1. After a travel day Wednesday, the series shifts to Cleveland for Game 3 on Thursday.Freddy Peralta delivered in the clutch with six shutout innings Tuesday in Game 2.Mary DeCicco via Getty ImagesRamírez's error gets Tampa Bay's offense goingThe game went into the fourth inning in a scoreless tie as Peralta and Guardians rookie starter Parker Messick traded blows. But in the bottom of the frame, a heads-up challenge from the Rays and Ramírez's error opened the door for Tampa Bay.After Junior Caminero drew a walk, Victor Mesa Jr. hit into what was called a double play on the field for the would-be first and second outs of the inning. But the Rays correctly challenged that Nathaniel Lowe's foot wasn't on the bag, and the out at first base was overturned. This saved out proved critical.The Rays then put runners on the corners with two outs, and Ben Williamson hit a ground ball to third base that should have ended the inning. But Ramírez let the ball slip through his legs, allowing Williamson to reach safely, Chandler Simpson to advance to third and Mesa to score. The Rays are on the board after this costly error by José Ramírez at third basepic.twitter.com/H08DzK78jV— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 14, 2026 One pitch later, Liam Hicks scored Simpson from third and Williamson from second with a line drive to right-center field.The Rays strike first in Game 2 with a 3-run inning! pic.twitter.com/piFVhwbIIV— MLB (@MLB) October 14, 2026 Just like that, the Rays had a 3-0 lead on three unearned runs. Those three runs turned out to be more than enough. Freddy Peralta delivers on promise of midseason tradeWhile Messick's line got hit with tough-luck runs, Peralta's remained pristine. He got through five scoreless innings on 85 pitches, which allowed him to come back out for the sixth.After he secured the first two outs of the frame, chants of "Freddy, Freddy, Freddy" rung out in the Tropicana Field stands. Peralta responded with a swinging strikeout of Petey Halpin to close out the sixth inning and maintain the shutout.Freddy Peralta pounds his chest after completing 6 scoreless innings 😤 pic.twitter.com/NwJsrLfpjX— MLB (@MLB) October 14, 2026 Peralta finished his day allowing 4 hits, 2 walks and 0 runs with 6 strikeouts and a chest pound as he walked off the mound. Tampa Bay's bullpen did the rest to ensure that his effort didn't go to waste. The high-stakes effort continued a remarkable turnaround for Peralta, who struggled along with many of his Mets teammates in the first half of the season but has gotten back on track in Tampa.In 22 starts with the Mets, Peralta posted a 4.99 ERA and 1.478 WHIP. This was one season removed from a 2025 All-Star campaign with the Milwaukee Brewers. Even so, the Rays acquired Peralta at the trade deadline to bolster their rotation for what they hoped would be a deep postseason run. He showed immediate improvement in Tampa and finished the season with a 3.25 ERA and 1.012 WHIP in 10 starts with his new team. On Tuesday, he delivered the exact type of postseason game the Rays were counting on when they acquired him.

articles.title: Rays Beat Guardians in Game 2 to Tie ALCS, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
articles.summary: The ALCS is all evened up.
articles.body:
After dropping Game 1 at home, the Tampa Bay Rays downed the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 thanks to a costly error and strong showing from the bottom half of their lineup. The series will head to Cleveland for Game 3 on Thursday.

Breaking down why Brewers can stop Dodgers 3-peat

Both offenses had a slow start, going scoreless through the first three-and-a-half innings, but Tampa Bay broke things open in the top of the fourth.

Junior Caminero got on base with a walk, but was thrown out on a fielder's choice, leaving Victor Mesa Jr. on first with one out. After Jonny DeLuca struck out, Chandler Simpson hit a two-out single to keep the inning alive and move Mesa to third, and Mesa managed to score on a fielding error.

Liam Hicks then hit a single to center field to drive in a pair of runs and give the Rays a 3-0 lead.

The Guardians didn't respond until the seventh when Chase DeLauter drove in a run with a double.

The Rays stranded two Cleveland runners on base, though, keeping a two-run lead heading into the stretch. The Guardians followed up the seventh by going down in order in the eighth inning.

The Guardians' defense did its part, getting six straight outs to avoid any more damage in the seventh or eighth innings, but Cleveland's offense never woke back up, going down in order in the top of the ninth.

While the Guardians would have liked to take a 2-0 lead on Tuesday, they managed to steal Game 1 on the road and will have the chance to regain the lead in the series at home on Thursday.

articles.body: The American League Championship Series has pitted two of the most unlikely franchises against each other, with a trip to the World Series on the line. The Tampa Bay Rays entered the 2026 season with one of the three lowest payrolls in baseball, as they usually do. They made few big additions, preferring to trust their farm system, player development staff, and the ability to mix and match players in specific situations. Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians found a way to reduce spending even further, running the lowest payroll in Major League Baseball, in order to maximize profits for team ownership. Fast-forward to October, and the Rays and Guardians are the two AL teams, not the Yankees or Red Sox. Not the Astros and Rangers from big markets in Texas. Or the Blue Jays, with their top-5 payroll, or even Detroit, where the Tigers ran the 11th highest payroll in baseball and by far the highest in the AL Central. DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS As surprising as it comes, if you haven't watched baseball before. But maybe even more surprising? How game one of the ALCS between these two teams played out. Cleveland, hardly known as an offensive powerhouse, fell behind 2-0 against one of the best run prevention teams in baseball. Then, starting in the sixth inning, they started scoring and never stopped. Home runs from Chase DeLauter and light-hitting catcher Patrick Bailey tied it, and a parade of hits led to a 4-3 lead in the eighth, which they promptly expanded to 7-3 by the ninth. The team that finished 24th in the league in runs scored, exploding for seven runs in game one of the ALCS against one of the best pitching staffs in baseball. If that doesn't demonstrate the randomness of postseason baseball, it's hard to know what does. Cleveland countered with Parker Messick, coming off an outstanding season of his own. But on Tuesday, Peralta, despite his struggles in New York, was electric. And he got a little help from his defense too, as star third baseman Junior Caminero made a nice play on a liner to his left, and hit the Dikembe Mutombo finger wag afterward. Just as you'd expect from the Tampa pitching lab, Peralta's start lowered his ERA to just 0.81 over his last eight starts in a Rays uniform. Somehow, they do it every single time. On offense, the Rays' lineup got to Messick in the fourth thanks to some shaky Cleveland defense. articles.title: Freddy Peralta, Liam Hicks lift Rays to 3-1 win over Guardians, evening the ALCS at 1-1
articles.summary: Freddy Peralta threw six innings of four-hit ball, Liam Hicks lined a two-run single after José Ramírez's fielding error and the Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 Tuesday night to even the AL Championship Series at 1-1.
articles.body: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — With the crowd chanting his name, a fired-up Freddy Peralta pumped one fastball after another past hitters all night long. Peralta threw six innings of four-hit ball, Liam Hicks lined a two-run single after José Ramírez's fielding error and the Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 Tuesday night to even the AL Championship Series at 1-1. Game 3 of the best-of-seven series is Thursday night in Cleveland. Peralta threw the hardest pitch of his big league career at 99.4 mph and relied on his four-seam fastball on 71 of 99 pitches — his 71.7% usage was his highest since June 11, 2019. “It’s no secret that I trust in my fastball a lot and it’s my best pitch,” Peralta said. Peralta's 96.9 mph average fastball velocity was 2.6 mph above his season average. “It plays a big role, the adrenaline,” Peralta said. “And also I define myself as a competitor, and I like these kind of games. I’ve always said in the past, that I enjoyed this as a Dominican pitcher. I grew up watching the games in D.R., and that’s the game that you see. And I got used to that because I grew up watching it. And I feel that I have that in me, in myself. And that’s the way that I feel when I am on the mound in these kind of games.” Peralta pumped a fist and screamed joyfully walking off the mound in the sixth after fanning Petey Halpin swinging at a 3-2 changeup. “I just enjoyed the moment because it was a really good at-bat,” Peralta said. “It wasn’t an easy game since the first pitch that I threw until the last one. It was a lot of competition between me and the hitters. ... I think that was why I was fired up like that.” Ramírez, whose two-run homer in Game 5 of their AL Division Series against Chicago helped the Guardians become the 11th team to overcome an 0-2 deficit in a best-of-five series, misplayed a grounder in the fourth inning that led to three unearned runs against rookie lefty Parker Messick. Junior Caminero walked to start that inning and Victor Mesa Jr. grounded into a forceout originally ruled a double play. The Rays challenged the calls at both first and second and Mesa was ruled safe when a video review overturned the out decision by first base umpire Mark Ripperger. After Jonny DeLuca struck out, Chandler Simpson beat out a high chopper to shortstop, and the Mesa reached third standing up when Ramírez failed to cover the bag. Ben Williamson followed with a grounder that scooted underneath Ramírez’s glove and between his legs after the ball hit the edge where the artificial turf met the infield dirt. The third baseman played back rather than charging. “It's a little bit faster here this type of surface,” Ramirez said through a translator. “It's frustrating. I feel bad.” Williamson reached second and Simpson went to third. Hicks drove the next pitch to right-center for a 3-0 lead, electrifying the towel-waving, cowbell-ringing crowd of 32,125 fans at Tropicana Field. Peralta and three relievers didn’t need any more support. “I think the velocity really stood out,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said of Peralta. Kevin Kelly got two outs in the seventh, retiring Ramírez on a fly ball to center with two runners on. Lefty Ian Seymour replaced him and Chase DeLauter lined an RBI double to the right-field corner. Seymour struck out Jo Adell swinging at a changeup, leaving runners at second and third. Seymour pitched a 1-2-3 eighth and Bryan Baker finished with a perfect ninth for his fourth postseason save. Acquired by the Rays from the Mets at the trade deadline, Peralta turned around his season in Tampa Bay, going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after posting a 4.99 ERA for New York. He pitched his latest gem in front of Mets owner Steve Cohen, who was in attendance. “We have a good relationship,” Peralta said of Cohen. “I think he’s awesome. And I’m happy that he was here watching, not watching me, watching the Rays.” Messick, who grew up going to Rays games at the Trop, took the loss after giving up six hits and the three unearned runs in five innings. Cleveland had won four straight in the postseason for the first time since winning their first six playoff games in 2016 on the way to a World Series berth. The 98-win Rays swept the New York Yankees before a 7-3 loss in Game 1 on Monday. That was their first loss in two weeks. Now, they're back on the winning track and need three more in a series that's reduced to a best of five to advance to their third World Series. Liam's lineup drop After batting cleanup in the first two games against the Yankees and sixth in Game 3 of that series, Hicks wasn't in the lineup against lefty Foster Griffin on Monday and batted eighth against Messick. He doesn't care where he hits. “This lineup is so good, you can hit anywhere in the lineup, and you’re not getting offended,” Hicks said. “There’s going to be opportunities.” No hit for you Caminero leaped to his left to snag Steven Kwan's hard liner to third in the fifth and then wagged a finger toward the batter. Caminero, who played all 162 games in the regular season and hit 42 home runs, was in the lineup after a collision with DeLuca on a foul ball in the ninth inning Monday night.
