articles.title: Freddy Peralta goes back to his roots, leans on 4-seam fastball to shut down the Guardians in Rays' ALCS-tying victory
articles.summary: Seventy-one of the 99 pitches Peralta threw in Game 2 were four-seamers — his highest usage in a start since 2019.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Fastball Freddy came out firing.

Coming off a frustrating Game 1 loss to the Cleveland Guardians , Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta was tasked with getting top-seeded Tampa Bay back on track in the American League Championship Series. When the Rays acquired Peralta from the New York Mets ahead of the trade deadline , these were the starts they had in mind.

Such visions were also predicated on Peralta rediscovering his best self after posting a 4.99 ERA across 22 starts as a Met. Little about his brief stint in Queens resembled the frontline starter whose fantastic four-seam fastball made him a two-time All-Star with Milwaukee.

It took some time. Peralta allowed seven runs in his first outing as a Ray at Coors Field, and he posted a 5.09 ERA over his three starts after that. But down the stretch, the impact version of Peralta resurfaced. Thanks to some key tweaks involving his delivery — raising his arm angle and restoring his elite extension down the mound — plus an uptick in changeup usage, things started to click again. Most importantly, these adjustments enabled the rejuvenation of his signature four-seamer. Across his final six regular-season starts, Peralta allowed just three runs in 34 innings (0.79 ERA), and he pitched well last round against the New York Yankees (4 ⅔ IP, 1 ER).

On Tuesday at Tropicana Field, with the Rays needing an ace-like performance against a Guardians lineup suddenly brimming with confidence, Peralta delivered the headlining effort in Tampa Bay's 3-1 victory to even the series . The stat line — 6 scoreless innings, 4 hits, 2 walks, 6 strikeouts — speaks for itself. And the style in which the pending free agent blitzed Cleveland's batters was reminiscent of the live-armed 21-year-old who burst on the scene with the Milwaukee Brewers back in 2018. It was the kind of performance that reminded everyone why he earned the "Fastball Freddy" moniker in the first place.

Peralta made all kinds of history in his major-league debut eight years ago, allowing just one hit across 5 ⅔ scoreless innings while striking out 13 Colorado Rockies. But the most notable element of his debut was found not in the box score but in the data: Of Peralta's 98 pitches, 90 were labeled four-seam fastballs by Statcast. It was an absurd breakdown, and it was reflective of Peralta's most special trait. Remarkably, it wasn't until he arrived in the majors that the righty fully grasped what that singular offering was capable of.

"I started learning about it when I got to the big leagues … and I started seeing the Trackman and all that," Peralta said. "When I started thinking about it, I knew that I had [gotten] a lot of pop-ups my whole career in the minors, a lot of swing-and-miss. But I had no idea about how special it was going to be."

Although he never replicated that level of lopsided usage, Peralta leaned on his four-seamer nearly 80% of the time during his first two big-league seasons. As he blossomed into a fully-formed frontline starter for Milwaukee, the fastball usage dipped closer to 50%, with his changeup and curveball emerging as dependable secondary offerings.

But on Tuesday in Game 2, Peralta went back to his roots. Twenty-six of his first 30 tosses were four-seam fastballs. The changeup emerged as a valuable weapon later in the outing, and the curveball made a handful of cameos, but by the end of the night, 71 of Peralta's 99 pitches were four-seamers — his highest usage (72%) in a start since 2019.

"Probably from pitch one," catcher Liam Hicks said afterward of when he knew Peralta could lean on his heater in Game 2. "It was unreal tonight. We definitely could tell by some of the swings early on, and the command he had with it today was pretty unbelievable."

In the first inning, Peralta rushed three fastballs past Chase DeLauter to give the standout Guardians rookie his first strikeout of the postseason. Three more punchouts followed in the second. A 95.9-mph fastball zipped past Nathaniel Lowe at the top of the zone before Peralta made Petey Halpin and Brayan Rocchio look foolish with a pair of changeups low and away as they tried to gear up for the high-90s heat.

Cleveland starter Parker Messick matched Peralta's zeroes through three innings but endured a series of unfortunate events that put the Rays on the board in the fourth. After Junior Caminero drew a leadoff walk, Victor Mesa Jr. appeared to ground into a double play but was ruled safe at first upon review. Messick struck out Jonny DeLuca for the second out, but then the speedy Chandler Simpson reached on an infield single to put runners on the corners for Ben Williamson.

Williamson tapped a seemingly harmless grounder toward third baseman José Ramírez, but the ball hit the lip of the infield grass and skipped under Ramírez's glove and through his legs to allow Mesa to score, Simpson to advance to third and Williamson to reach second. Then the lefty-swinging Hicks — moved down to eighth in the batting order against a tough southpaw in Messick — jumped on a first-pitch slider to drive in two more and make it 3-0 Rays. Paired with his single to lead off the third, it marked just the second game this season in which Hicks notched multiple hits against a lefty.

In the fifth, the Guardians started to pressure Peralta. With two outs, Ramírez singled and stole second, then DeLauter walked. That brought the powerful Jo Adell to the plate as the tying run. But after a mound visit from pitching coach Kyle Snyder, Peralta found a new gear to escape the trouble.

Before Adell stepped into the box, Peralta had thrown 11,350 four-seam fastballs as a major-leaguer. His 11,351st was his fastest yet: 99.4 mph right down the middle, which Adell fouled off for strike one. Peralta reared back and attacked again with 99 mph — a mark he had reached only five times in his career prior to Tuesday — and got Adell to fly out to center field to end the frame.

"It plays a big role, the adrenaline," Peralta said postgame when asked about his personal best against Adell. "And also, I define myself as a competitor — and I like these kinds of games."

To punctuate his outing and finish his sixth frame, Peralta won a nine-pitch battle with Halpin by coaxing another chase on the changeup for his sixth strikeout. With that, he completed six innings for the first time in his postseason career.

A DeLauter RBI double in the seventh spoiled Tampa Bay's shutout, but the bullpen held on from there, and All-Star closer Bryan Baker nailed down his fourth save of the postseason to seal the Rays' Game 2 victory and tie the ALCS.

"I think his fastball-changeup combo is one of the best in the game," Baker said of Peralta. "Whatever tweaks they worked on, it's paying off big-time. I think the fastball was even livelier today — he was probably pretty amped up in this scenario.

articles.title: Pathway Opens For Mets To Land Tarik Skubal
articles.summary: One of baseball’s major storylines this season was solved when the Detroit Tigers traded ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, who had won consecutive American League Cy...
articles.body:
One of baseball's major storylines this season was solved when the Detroit Tigers traded ace pitcher Tarik Skubal, who had won consecutive American League Cy Young Awards, to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Skubal is in the midst of a playoff run with the Dodgers, trying to help them become the first team in over a quarter century to win three straight World Series championships.

He's also slated to become an unrestricted free agent at this season's send, and could potentially command a new contract worth upwards of $400 million.

But will he return to the Dodgers, or seek greener (and more expensive) pastures elsewhere? According to a key MLB Insider, Skubal's next destination may already be known.

The New York Mets Will Reportedly Match Any Offer Tarik Skubal Gets On The Open Free Agency Market

According to a report from SNY MLB Insider Chelsea Janes, the New York Mets are expected to match whatever offer Skubal may receive elsewhere in free agency during the offseason.

Skubal choosing the Mets in free agency makes sense in the mind of Bleacher Report's Zachary Rymer, considering that the Dodgers and Yankees already have established starting rotations, something the Mets need strengthening with.

"At that rate, the Skubal sweepstakes could come down to which of the Mets, Dodgers, or Yankees would be most willing to take the risk. And of those three clubs, the Mets may have the clearest need for a No. 1 starter this winter," Rymer wrote.

Will Mets team owner David Stearns be willing to shell out the money to land Skubal? Considering what he paid to sign Juan Soto, it's possible.

"Whether David Stearns would want to shell out so much money for Skubal is a fair question, but what he wants might not matter if Steve Cohen decides to step in," Rymer added. "He notably did so to land Juan Soto on a 15-year, $765 million deal."

Tarik Skubal Was Acquired By The Dodgers From The Tigers

As part of their trade of Skubal to the Dodgers in early August, the Detroit Tigers received a trio of prospects in return, including right-handed arm River Ryan.

Skubal's credentials are well-established, as he won consecutive AL Cy Young Awards and is in line for a major contract this offseason.

articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who won consecutive World Series titles and are trying for a third, acquired ace pitcher Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in early August in return for a trio of prospects.

Right now, the Dodgers and Skubal are in a perilous position, as they trail the National League Championship Series, two games to none to the Milwaukee Brewers with Game 3 on deck for Wednesday evening.

But regardless of how this series turns out, Skubal will be a free agent in the offseason and could potentially be in line for a contract worth upwards of $400 million. Are the Dodgers going to do what's necessary to keep him, or will another team swoop in and grab him off the open market?

Los Angeles Dodgers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Could Land With The Mets, Per New Reports

According to a new report from SNY MLB Insider Chelsea Janes, the New York Mets are expected to match whatever offer that Skubal receives on the open market.

Meanwhile, this would correlate with what Bleacher Report's Zachary Rymer recently wrote, considering that the Dodgers and New York Yankees already have established starting rotations, something the Mets are looking to strengthen.

"At that rate, the Skubal sweepstakes could come down to which of the Mets, Dodgers, or Yankees would be most willing to take the risk. And of those three clubs, the Mets may have the clearest need for a No. 1 starter this winter," Rymer wrote.

"Whether (Mets owner) David Stearns would want to shell out so much money for Skubal is a fair question, but what he wants might not matter if Steve Cohen decides to step in," Rymer added. "He notably did so to land Juan Soto on a 15-year, $765 million deal."

Tarik Skubal Was Acquired From The Tigers In August

Skubal, who is the reigning American League Cy Young Award winner in consecutive seasons, recently explained that he welcomes the pressure that comes with being a Dodgers pitcher.

"The pressure surrounding the Dodgers is a privilege. As an athlete, this is what you want to be and you want to have an expectation to win," Skubal said to Dodgers Nation's Noel Sanchez and media.

"I have those same expectations as a player and in my shoes, I think just keeping the game the game, going out there and competing and doing what I can to put my team in a position to win is important."

articles.title: Jacob Misiorowski, Junior Caminero and Every MLB Team's Best Player Under 25
articles.summary: All 30 MLB teams have at least one promising building block for the future, and with a wealth of young, rising talent across baseball, the future of the sport is in good hands.
articles.body:
All 30 MLB teams have at least one promising building block for the future, and with a wealth of young, rising talent across baseball, the future of the sport is in good hands.

Jacob Misiorowski (Brewers), Junior Caminero (Rays), Chase DeLauter (Guardians) and Edgardo Henriquez (Dodgers) are all still in action and hoping to help their teams reach the World Series.

With that in mind, we set out to identify the best under-25 player on every MLB roster during the 2026 season. Ages reflect how old a player was on June 30, which is the standard for how season ages are presented on Baseball Reference, FanGraphs and other sites.

The focus was solely on this year's production, so long-term potential was not part of the equation, and only major league contributions were considered.

Age: 24 Stats: 132 G, 112 OPS+, .228/.297/.461, 45 XBH (24 HR), 1.1 WAR

Terrific batted-ball metrics make it easy to believe in Mayo's ability to make an above-average offensive impact, even with a middling on-base percentage and strikeout rate above 30 percent. He is stretched defensively at third base (568.2 INN, -9 DRS) and blocked by Pete Alonso at first base, so primary designated hitter could be his role in 2027.

Age: 23 Stats: 26 GS, 9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP, 2.9 WAR

Most would have expected Roman Anthony to be the guy here going into the season, but injuries limited him to 55 games. Meanwhile, Tolle emerged as a frontline-caliber starter in his first full season in the majors. Over his final 10 starts, he had a 2.59 ERA, 1.08 WHIP and 75 strikeouts in 59 innings.

Age: 21 Stats: 42 G, 92 OPS+, .237/.285/.414, 12 XBH (7 HR), 1.1 WAR

Lombard made his MLB debut on Aug. 4, just a few months after his 21st birthday. He homered in his MLB debut and logged a .953 OPS over his first seven games before leveling off at the plate, but he provided strong defense (373.2 INN, 5 DRS) and some occasional pop. By season's end, he had pushed Anthony Volpe to a utility role.

Age: 22 Stats: 162 G, 144 OPS+, .276/.360/.524, 68 XBH (42 HR), 5.7 WAR

After a 45-homer, 110-RBI season in 2025, Caminero was a more well-rounded hitter in 2026. He raised his walk rate (6.3 to 11.3 percent) and on-base percentage (.311 to .360) while maintaining elite power production, and a top-five finish in AL MVP balloting is likely on the horizon.

Age: 22 Stats: 20 GS, 5-6, 3.69 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, 97 K, 97.2 IP, 2.0 WAR

After an impressive run in the 2025 postseason, Yesavage put together a strong rookie season while navigating injury issues. He started the season on the injured list with a shoulder impingement and underwent meniscus surgery in August, but when he did take the mound he looked the part of a long-term piece of Toronto's rotation puzzle.

Age: 24 Stats: 154 G, 115 OPS+, .276/.350/.415, 47 XBH (16 HR), 4.5 WAR

The future is bright for the White Sox thanks to a young core that includes Chase Meidroth (25), Sam Antonacci (23), Kyle Teel (24), Braden Montgomery (23), Grant Taylor (24), Hagen Smith (22) and Noah Schultz (22). Meidroth raised his OPS by 116 points in his second MLB season, and a .286/.364/.473 line after the All-Star break suggests there is more to come.

Age: 24 Stats: 133 G, 131 OPS+, .287/.363/.457, 49 XBH (16 HR), 3.5 WAR

Injuries limited Chase DeLauter to 138 games over three full seasons in the minors, but he made his MLB debut during the 2025 postseason and broke camp with a spot on Cleveland's Opening Day roster. His 3.5 WAR trailed only Parker Messick (6.3) and Steven Kwan (5.3) for a Guardians team that is playing in the ALCS.

Age: 21 Stats: 156 G, 126 OPS+, .278/.376/.430, 51 XBH (18 HR), 7.1 WAR

McGonigle burst onto the scene and led the AL with 7.1 WAR, emerging as an immediate offensive star and a standout defender at both shortstop and third base. He had almost as many walks (95) as strikeouts (100), and found more in-game power as the season unfolded with 10 home runs in 63 games after the All-Star break.

Age: 23 Stats: 143 G, 132 OPS+, .289/.340/.494, 57 XBH (23 HR), 3.2 WAR

Caglianone had a 47 OPS+ and negative-1.3 WAR over 62 games in his MLB debut, but he broke through as a legitimate middle-of-the-order run producer in his first full season. He hit .337/.373/.549 with 25 extra-base hits in 53 games after the All-Star break, earning the nod here over Carter Jensen (120 OPS+, 27 HR, 64 XBH, 3.3 WAR).

Age: 23 Stats: 152 G, 120 OPS+, .282/.374/.407, 42 XBH (10 HR), 2.2 WAR

Keaschall started the year at second base and saw some sporadic action in center field before settling in as Minnesota's primary right fielder. He had an .897 OPS and 23 extra-base hits with a .411 on-base percentage after the All-Star break, and looks like a legitimate long-term building block on a retooling Minnesota roster.

Stats: 99 G, 141 OPS+, .256/.396/.483, 37 XBH (21 HR), 3.7 WAR

Kurtz saw his season end prematurely on July 31 with a thumb injury, and he was one of several key offensive pieces to miss significant time for the Athletics in 2026. Despite playing just 99 games, he was still a 3.7-WAR player, and his 141 OPS+ helped further legitimize his terrific rookie production.

Stats: 157 G, 87 OPS+, .210/.279/.390, 44 XBH (21 HR), 1.0 WAR

With 139 starts in right field, Smith was the one constant in an otherwise unstable Houston outfield. His 88 OPS+ in 1,061 plate appearances over the last two seasons raises questions about whether he was rushed to the majors, but he took a meaningful step forward this year with more playable power (21 HR) and an improved strikeout rate (27.8 to 26.1 percent).

Stats: 27 GS, 9-11, 2.97 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 142 K, 148.1 IP, 3.8 WAR

Ureña began the year as a surprise member of the Opening Day roster and pitching in a relief role, but he joined the starting rotation in mid-April and ended up putting together a fantastic rookie campaign. His 3.62 FIP and .210 opponents' batting average speak to the quality of his stuff, and he could be the team's Opening Day starter next year if Reid Detmers is traded.

Stats: 160 G, 99 OPS+, .246/.312/.381, 40 XBH (17 HR), 4.4 WAR

With 16 Defensive Runs Saved, Young trailed only Brice Turang (23) among all second basemen, and that helped make him a 4.4-WAR player in his first full season in the majors. A .279/.388/.432 hitter in the minors often lauded for his advanced hit tool, he is capable of another step forward at the plate in 2027.

Stats: 110 G, 118 OPS+, .238/.333/.421, 39 XBH (17 HR), 3.5 WAR

Langford has quietly tallied 13.3 WAR in 378 games over the past three seasons, good for the eighth-highest total among outfielders during that stretch. Even with multiple trips to the injured list and only 110 games played this year, his 3.5 WAR was the second-highest mark on the Rangers' roster.

Ranking Top 25 Trade Chips For Offseason 🔢

Age: 21 Stats: 58 G, 3 SV, 18 HLD, 2.45 ERA, 1.11 WHIP, 11.3 K/9, 2.3 WAR

The fourth-youngest player to appear in a big league game in 2026, Fuentes emerged as a high-leverage arm at the back of the Atlanta bullpen alongside veterans Robert Suárez and Raisel Iglesias. With a fastball that regularly touches triple-digits and a slider that generated a 37.9 percent whiff rate, he could be the closer of the future if he doesn't return to a starting role.

Age: 23 Stats: 144 G, 122 OPS+, .295/.333/.458, 48 XBH (11 HR), 3.3 WAR

Sanoja saw the bulk of his action at third base, but also made a handful of starts at second base, shortstop and both corner outfield spots. He won the utility player Gold Glove a year ago, and more than doubled his WAR this season thanks to a 108-point increase in his OPS.

Age: 24 Stats: 31 GS, 12-10, 3.16 ERA, 1.17 WHIP, 194 K, 179.2 IP, 3.0 WAR

The Mets have a solid young core taking shape. Nolan McLean (24) and Carson Benge (23) are both NL Rookie of the Year candidates, while A.J. Ewing (21) and Zac Thornton (24) emerged as surprise MLB contributors. McLean was one of only seven pitchers with 20 quality starts, anchoring the Mets rotation after his run with Team USA in the World Baseball Classic.

Philadelphia Phillies: RHP Andrew Painter

Age: 23 Stats: 23 GS, 3-10, 5.40 ERA, 1.41 WHIP, 115 K, 126.2 IP, 1.3 WAR

Painter and center fielder Justin Crawford (149 G, 78 OPS+, .264/.309/.353, 27 XBH, 17 SB, -0.2 WAR) both won Opening Day roster spots and filled primary roles on a playoff-bound Phillies roster. Painter was the more productive player, and things started to click down the stretch when he logged a 3.27 ERA in 41.1 innings while tallying four quality starts in his last seven outings.

Age: 23 Stats: 135 G, 144 OPS+, .265/.388/.503, 61 XBH (30 HR), 3.7 WAR

CJ Abrams just wrapped up his age-25 season, making Wood the easy choice as the co-star of the Nationals' surprisingly potent offense. The towering 6'6" slugger also had 21 steals in 25 attempts, tallied 102 walks and made a modest improvement to his strikeout rate (32.1 to 28.7 percent) while recording his second straight 30-homer campaign.

Age: 24 Stats: 162 G, 156 OPS+, .280/.372/.570, 84 XBH (45 HR), 9.8 WAR

After a sluggish second half to a breakout 2025 season, PCA looked like a potential regression candidate. Instead, he is the presumptive NL MVP winner, and could take home the honor unanimously after a 9.8-WAR season where he had 45 home runs, 41 steals and played Platinum Glove-caliber defense in center field. He is now a bona fide superstar and the face of the franchise on the North Side.

Age: 24 Stats: 143 G, 142 OPS+, .283/.365/.515, 65 XBH (30 HR), 5.6 WAR

Chase Burns (23) and Sal Stewart (22) both put together breakout seasons to give the Reds two excellent young building blocks, but De La Cruz was the team's best all-around player by a comfortable margin. Aside from his established power/speed combination, he took a major step forward in his approach at the plate while also providing more reliable defense at shortstop.

Milwaukee Brewers: RHP Jacob Misiorowski

Age: 24 Stats: 30 GS, 16-5, 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 252 K, 174.2 IP, 6.5 WAR

The hardest-throwing starting pitcher perhaps ever, Misiorowski went from young pitcher prone to inconsistency to the NL Cy Young favorite and unquestioned ace of the Milwaukee staff in the wake of the Freddy Peralta trade. Outfielder Jackson Chourio (22) would be an easy choice for almost any other team, while Logan Henderson (24) and Cooper Pratt (21) also deserve a mention.

Age: 24 Stats: 32 GS, 10-11, 3.82 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, 200 K, 174.1 IP, 3.3 WAR

It speaks volumes that the above numbers represent a clear down year for Skenes, as they would be a career year for most pitchers. The Pirates will be banking on a return to Cy Young form next year, as he anchors a roster that also features Konnor Griffin (20), Bubba Chandler (23) and Esmerlyn Valdez (22) as impact players on the rise.

Age: 24 Stats: 158 G, 124 OPS+, .269/.327/.466, 62 XBH (29 HR), 3.3 WAR

After struggling to a 69 OPS+ and negative-2.5 WAR in exactly 162 games during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, this was likely a make-or-break season for Walker to maintain his hold on an everyday job. He responded with 29 home runs, 102 RBI and 22 steals while raising his OPS more than 200 points. The young double-play combination of JJ Wetherholt (23) and Masyn Winn (24) also deserves a mention.

Arizona Diamondbacks: OF Ryan Waldschmidt

Age: 23 Stats: 82 G, 94 OPS+, .256/.325/.368, 20 XBH (3 HR), 0.8 WAR

One of the oldest teams in baseball, the only notable contributors for the D-backs from the under-25 group were Waldschmidt and fellow former top prospect Jordan Lawlar. Waldschmidt played more games (82 to 44), while Lawlar was more productive when he did play (115 OPS+ to 94 OPS+). Both could be starters in the 2027 outfield.

Age: 24 Stats: 93 G, 112 OPS+, .279/.341/.477, 38 XBH (12 HR), 1.2 WAR

Carrigg was the starting shortstop for Team Israel in the World Baseball Classic but settled in as the primary center fielder in Colorado after making his MLB debut on June 9. He hit .327/.340/.571 with 11 extra-base hits in 101 plate appearances in September, and he should join Jake McCarthy and Mickey Moniak in a quietly productive Colorado outfield.

Los Angeles Dodgers: RHP Edgardo Henriquez

Age: 24 Stats: 61 G, 2 SV, 11 HLD, 2.85 ERA, 1.03 WHIP, 10.7 K/9, 0.8 WAR

A high-octane relief arm who averages 100.7 mph with his fastball and backs it with a wipeout slider that generated a 43.2 percent whiff rate, Henriquez steadily pitched his way into a key role at the back of the Dodgers bullpen. He allowed just 37 hits in 60 innings of work, limiting opposing hitters to a .177 batting average. He has the stuff to be the closer of the future.

Age: 23 Stats: 158 G, 105 OPS+, .254/.303/.440, 57 XBH (26 HR), 3.4 WAR

After an ugly start to the season, Merrill hit .304/.339/.569 with 16 home runs and 49 RBI in 65 games after the All-Star break, and he was instrumental in the team's late-season surge to a wild-card berth. He does not turn 24 years old until the first month of the 2027 season, but already has 10.6 WAR across three full MLB seasons.

Age: 21 Stats: 107 G, 133 OPS+, .269/.364/.461, 40 XBH (17 HR), 2.1 WAR

Eldridge went 3-for-28 with 13 strikeouts in his first taste of the big leagues as a September call-up in 2025, and he started the year back at Triple-A Sacramento. Once he was recalled in early May, it was clear he had made the necessary adjustments, and by season's end he was hitting No. 3 in the batting order. The 6'7" slugger has some of the best raw power in baseball, and his 17 home runs in 107 games are just the tip of the iceberg.

articles.title: Buyer Beware: Which MLB Free Agents Should Teams Avoid?
articles.summary: While Tarik Skubal is the clear belle of the ball in this winter's MLB free agency cycle, there will be dozens of players who get multi-year contracts at north of $10M per season.
articles.body:
While Tarik Skubal is the clear belle of the ball in this winter's MLB free agency cycle, there will be dozens of players who get multi-year contracts at north of $10M per season.

In pursuit of this offseason's versions of Pete Alonso and Dylan Cease, however, teams are hoping they don't drive off the metaphorical used car lot in a lemon.

Every player on this list was worth at least 2.0 WAR in 2026, according to either FanGraphs or Baseball-Reference (though not necessarily both). Notably, each and every one of the 24 players who were worth at least 2.0 fWAR before hitting free agency last winter ended up getting eight-figure salaries on their new contracts.

Some of them proved to be more than worth it in 2026, but quite a few emphatically were not.

Who are this year's looming busts to avoid?

To be clear, every player on this list deserves to sign somewhere. Most should get at least double their 2026 salary, too.

But the teams that win these forthcoming bidding wars may live to regret it.

2026 Stats : 174.1 IP, 3.77 ERA, 4.47 FIP, 1.10 WHIP, 9.0 K/9

Since making his MLB debut in 2024, Shota Imanaga has pitched 492.1 innings, posting a 3.45 ERA and a 5.11 K/BB ratio.

There is one pitcher in all of baseball with more innings pitched, a lower ERA and a higher K/BB ratio during that time. His name is Tarik Skubal—546.0, 2.42 and 6.89, respectively.

The problem is that among the 80 pitchers with at least 350 innings pitched since the beginning of 2024, no one has a worse ratio of home runs allowed per nine innings pitched than Imanaga's mark of 1.70.

It's only because of Aaron Nola that Imanaga didn't "lead" the majors in home runs allowed in 2026. It's only because he missed nearly two months of action that he wasn't dead last in that department in 2025.

Even worse, the home run monster always becomes more problematic for Imanaga in the latter months of the season. If you include his postseason numbers from last fall, he has allowed 42 home runs in 178.2 innings pitched (2.12 HR/9) from August 1 onward.

Signing with either San Francisco or St. Louis could help alleviate the issue, as Oracle Park and Busch Stadium have consistently been two of MLB's least homer-happy venues over the past three years. But what happens when you need him to keep the ball in the park at Dodger Stadium or Yankee Stadium in October?

2026 Stats : .266/.389/.484, 26 HR, 86 RBI, 11 SB

Jake Bauers is probably going to get some down-ballot votes for NL MVP, and deservedly so. The man led the 103-win Brewers in home runs, walks and OPS.

But where in the world did this come from?

From 2018-25, Bauers had a minus-1.2 bWAR and a minus-0.4 fWAR. In fact, among the 252 players who received at least 1,900 plate appearances during that time, only late-career Miguel Cabrera had a worse fWAR than Bauers.

This, of course, begs the question: What does history say about hitters who suddenly break through at the age of 30 after plenty of opportunity to do so in their 20s?

A prime example from recent history is Justin Smoak, who spent seven replacement-level seasons in the big leagues before becoming an All-Star out of nowhere at 30. He proceeded to have a respectable enough age-31 campaign, but his breakthrough year was more of a one-hit wonder than any sort of second-half-of-career rebirth.

Is Bauers destined for a similar fate? Or is this more of a "going to shine for a few years after a late arrival" situation?

For $2.7M, Bauers was an incredible bargain this year. We'll see how things go from here.

2026 Stats : 116.0 IP, 3.41 ERA, 3.19 FIP, 1.09 WHIP, 8.8 K/9

Michael Soroka had a solid season in the desert.

He was one of just 13 pitchers to log at least 110 innings with an ERA of 3.50 or better, a WHIP of 1.10 or better and a K/9 of 8.5 or better. His cohorts in that club were: Jacob Misiorowski, Dylan Cease, Cam Schlittler, Chris Sale, Tarik Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Jesús Luzardo, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Drew Rasmussen, Parker Messick, Reid Detmers and Payton Tolle.

Soroka also just turned 29 this summer. The other 29-year-old free agent in that group (Skubal) is probably headed to a record-setting contract.

However, yet again, Soroka could not stay healthy.

He missed nearly two months with a glute injury and subsequently missed two more weeks of action with shoulder inflammation.

That would be a nothing burger if he had been generally healthy in recent years, but it was the first time Soroka had pitched 90 innings in a season since 2019.

That's why he signed with Arizona to a one-year, $7.5M deal with up to $2M in appearance incentives, one year after earning a $9M contract with Washington. If a team could get him again on a deal in that vicinity, it would be a no-brainer.

Spotrac puts his market value at $56.4M for four years, which would be quite the ill-advised gamble for any team to take.

2026 Stats : .231/.312/.399, 19 HR, 55 RBI, 41 SB

Over the previous half-decade, Jazz Chisholm Jr. had been a considerably better-than-average hitter against fastballs. No one was confusing him with Aaron Judge or Shohei Ohtani, but he had a .508 slugging percentage against the collection of four-seamers, sinkers and cutters—on par with the likes of Bobby Witt Jr. and Corbin Carroll.

This year, however, his barrel rate plummeted. He ended up with a run value against fastballs that ranked in the bottom five percent among qualified hitters.

After posting actual and expected slugging percentages of .481 in 2025, Chisholm finished with .399 and .366 in 2026, respectively.

The glass-half-full perspective is that even in a down year by his standards, Chisholm still racked up 19 home runs and 41 stolen bases. (Plus four more swipes in the postseason.) Seasons like those don't grow on trees, especially among second basemen. Maybe his barrel rate bounces back after an underwhelming walk year.

But what if struggling with fastballs is simply his new normal?

Can anyone justify giving him anything close to the sort of $300M contract he thought he was worth heading into this season?

If that market never comes together and he settles for something like a one-year, $25M deal with a $22M player option for a second season, that might be a bargain. Any sort of contract that goes into the 2030s, however, is a terrifying proposition.

2026 Stats : 172.2 IP, 3.60 ERA, 3.96 FIP, 1.21 WHIP, 8.2 K/9

Generally speaking, starting pitchers who hit free agency the winter after an All-Star Game make bank.

No one fit that description last year, save for the retiring Clayton Kershaw. The two who did so in 2024 were Corbin Burnes and Max Fried. They. both signed for north of $200M. This year, there are three: Tarik Skubal, Nick Martinez (who would be a strong candidate for a huge payday if he weren't already 36 years old) and Foster Griffin.

To be sure, it's a "one of these things is not like the other" situation. By no means is Griffin coming within a thousand miles of Burnes/Fried/Skubal money. But he'll surely get a raise from his $5.5M salary this year.

Will it be regrettable for the team that signs him?

En route to being named an All-Star, Griffin had a 2.77 ERA in the first half. He was particularly on point in June, allowing four runs over five starts with 33 strikeouts against just four walks.

His final 10 starts of the regular season were a much different story, though, posting a 5.73 ERA.

Maybe he just ran out of good luck? After a .249 BABIP against through his first 21 starts, it skyrocketed to a .382 mark for the rest of the season.

Perhaps he simply hit a wall? Griffin averaged just 116 innings pitched over his previous three seasons in Japan. After 124 innings, things started to go downhill.

Or maybe opponents figured him out as they got more tape on him?

Griffin's whiff rate plummeted in August. Then, opponents hit .560 against his go-to pitch (the cutter) in September.

The silver lining is that he wasn't getting tattooed. In fact, Griffin didn't allow a single home run across his final six starts of the regular season. Still, base hit followed base hit as regression from the strong first half reared its ugly head.

2026 Stats : .295/.363/.502, 21 HR, 72 RBI

Ty France's 2026 stat line was almost identical to what Josh Naylor did before hitting free agency last year: a .295 batting average and 20 home runs.

Naylor stole way more bags (30). France has the substantially better glove at first base. France is four years older than Naylor was last October. Still, it's a noteworthy comparison between a guy who made $2M this season and one who got a five-year, $92.5M contract last winter.

With Naylor, though, that level of production was nothing new. He hit 31 home runs the season before his walk year. He batted .308 the year before that.

But France couldn't hit much of anything from 2023-25. He kept getting regular playing time, but among the 103 players who made at least 1,500 plate appearances in those three years, only Andrés Giménez, Anthony Volpe and Brenton Doyle had a worse OPS (.686).

Then again, from 2020-22, France was a .285 hitter who averaged 20 home runs per 162 games played.

So, did he find the fountain of youth in San Diego?

Or is he destined to go right back to replacement-level production on a new deal?

More importantly, how much is it going to cost to find out?

France has made a little north of $16M in his eight-year career, but his salary might be a bit north of $16M on a multi-year deal if Naylor, Christian Walker, José Abreu, Anthony Rizzo and Brandon Belt are reasonable comps for France's market.

He was worth 3.6 fWAR this season. Those first basemen were all in the 2.5-3.8 range in their walk year before getting AAVs ranging from $16M-$20M.

My guess is he'll be more in the two-year, $25M type of range, but even that would've been unthinkable six months ago and could age poorly.

2026 Stats : 149.0 IP, 3.99 ERA, 3.99 FIP, 1.24 WHIP, 8.3 K/9

Shortly after the trade deadline , MLB.com ranked the 25 biggest trades .

Tyler Mahle going to Atlanta didn't even crack the list, but it ended up being maybe the biggest non-Skubal trade of them all.

Mahle was masterful over the final two months of the regular season, making nine starts with a 1.99 ERA. He proceeded to deliver two more quality starts in the postseason. He was the only pitcher through two rounds who could make such a claim.

Based solely on the way he pitched down the stretch, he ought to be a top-five pitcher on the open market.

However, the reason Mahle's departure from San Francisco barely made a blip on the national radar was because he had a 5.13 ERA prior to the trade deadline. He could never seem to get or stay healthy over the previous four seasons.

Is he a legitimate No. 2 starter for a contender?

Or should he be viewed as a No. 4/5 starter who happens to enter free agency on a two-month tear?

Mahle signed a two-year, $22M deal when he hit free agency for the first time three years ago, as well as a one-year, $10M contract this past offseason. But he was recovering from Tommy John surgery the first time and had missed more than half of the 2025 campaign due to injury.

This is the first time teams are bidding on a reasonably healthy Mahle, and that might mean a considerable overpay is forthcoming.

articles.title: There are 4 teams left in MLB’s postseason. Who ultimately prevails could say a lot about the league’s future
articles.summary: This year’s NLCS rematch between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Milwaukee Brewers holds heavy stakes – for the two teams, and potentially the future of MLB.
articles.body: This year’s National League Championship Series (NLCS) rematch between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Milwaukee Brewers holds heavy stakes – for the two teams, and potentially the future of MLB. The high-priced Dodgers are setting their sights on becoming only the fifth team to ever three-peat while thrifty Milwaukee’s out for redemption on the way to their franchise’s second World Series appearance. The rest of the league is watching closely to see how the battle of payrolls shakes out. It’s no secret that the Dodgers have spared no expense in assembling one of baseball’s most-envied rosters. In just the last two years, the team won back-to-back championships and ranked among the league’s top three most expensive payrolls. Back in the NLCS this year, LA is the second-highest payroll in all of Major League Baseball, spending about $338 million. The Dodgers’ Midwestern opponent sits in the bottom half of the league when it comes to spending. With about $143 million on the books, the Brewers rank 19th in payroll. Before Game 1 of the NLCS was played, Brewers general manager Matt Arnold was asked about the premise of small market teams like Milwaukee not being able to compete with powerhouse franchises like Los Angeles and the two teams in New York. “Nobody here is worried about that right now,” Arnold answered. “We’re focused on trying to win, and I think we have for a while. Regardless of what the economics look like, the guys in there believe, and so do I.” It makes sense for them to believe. Going into Wednesday’s Game 3, the Brewers have a commanding 2-0 lead in the series. With the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) between the league and the players’ association set to expire in December, the biggest topic of conversation surrounding upcoming negotiations has been the league’s proposal to implement a salary cap and floor. It’s a potentially monumental shift for MLB, the only major American sports league without a salary cap. Front offices with wealthier owners would no longer be able to throw the bag at players with no regard for the bottom line (aside from the league’s luxury tax). Stars would be spread out more evenly across the league. Scouting and developmental programs would become overwhelmingly vital overnight. A salary cap would introduce a fundamental change to the way teams are built. And three of the four teams remaining in the postseason might just be giving the rest of the league the blueprint on how to do it. While the Dodgers’ deep pockets have come with consistent success, this year might prove that teams don’t need to break the bank to build World Series-ready rosters. After the Brewers’ two wins to open the NLCS, the Dodgers trail in a postseason series for the first time since 2024. But it’s not just the cost-effective top-seeded team in the National League that Los Angeles needs to worry about – the American League has two thrifty contenders that could also pose a threat to the defending champions’ reign. The Cleveland Guardians advanced to the ALCS while spending just over $74 million, ranking dead last in payroll league wide. The fourth team in World Series contention, the Tampa Bay Rays, stands just above the Guardians in payroll at 25th, with about $98 million on the books. Prior to the first game of the ALCS, Guardians manager Stephen Vogt praised the Tampa Bay and Cleveland general managers respectively. “Eric Neander and Chris Antonetti are two of the best people in baseball,” Vogt said. “And they’re really good at what they do – and building teams very differently than some of the teams around the league.” The three non-Dodgers teams remaining in the postseason all spent less than half of what LA did on its personnel. The Brewers’, Guardians’ and Rays’ total salaries combined ($315 million) still come out to less than the Dodgers’ $338 million. With a possible salary cap coming, teams might be looking closely at the other three going forward rather than the Dodger way. Throughout the year, these frugal teams have accomplished quite a bit while matching up against the league’s high rollers. The Brewers finished the season with the best record among all 30 teams, entering the postseason with 103 regular-season wins. The Rays had the best record in the American League. The bargain Guardians clinched the American League Central title and earned a bye in the playoffs. Meanwhile, this year has seen some pricey teams peter out early. The most expensive team in baseball, the New York Mets, didn’t see the postseason this year. The fifth-highest payroll, the Toronto Blue Jays – seen as serious competitors for the AL East title – saw their season end before October. The New York Yankees, the third-most expensive team in the league and a trendy pick to win the World Series, were swept by the Rays in the ALDS. The Brewers, Rays and Guardians aren’t the flashiest of teams. They don’t primarily rely on big-name sluggers but rather believe in the kind of analytics that lead to the front office emphasizing players with contact skills that put the ball in play. Fundamental fielding, smart baserunning and the entire roster, top to bottom, are necessary for their success. “Good teams do not rely on just one or two people,” Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash said after their Game 2 ALDS win against the Yankees. “We rely on all nine in the lineup, the guys on the bench and certainly our entire pitching staff.” So far, it’s translated to wins.

articles.title: Jose Ramirez Takes Blame for Guardians' ALCS G2 Loss to Rays After Mistakes, 'I Feel Bad About That'
articles.summary: Cleveland Guardians star José Ramírez owned up to his defensive misplay that helped give the Tampa Bay Rays the lead in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series.
articles.body:
Cleveland Guardians star José Ramírez owned up to his defensive misplay that helped give the Tampa Bay Rays the lead in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series.

Ramírez called his error "frustrating" and added that "I feel bad about that."

"It's a little bit faster here with the surface and I was playing parallel to the base," he said through an interpreter, per ESPN.com . "The ball bounced right on the edge between the dirt and the turf, and that's what made it a little more difficult for me. I tried to knock it down."

The seven-time All-Star let a ground ball from Rays second baseman Ben Williamson get under him, which allowed one run to score. Catcher Liam Hicks came up next and hit a two-run single.

Instead of Cleveland getting out of the inning without allowing a run, it was down 3-0.

It didn't help that the offense went to sleep after scoring seven runs on 14 hits in Game 1. Designated hitter Chase DeLauter drove home the Guardians' only run with an RBI double in the seventh, and they combined to go 1-for-6 with runners in scoring position.

All things considered, heading to Progressive Field with the ALCS tied at 1-1 is a good position for Stephen Vogt's squad.

And if there's anybody who earned a pass for making a costly mistake, it's Ramírez. He's batting .333 and slugging .667 so far in the postseason.

The series resumes Thursday. Having a home crowd behind them should help the Guardians move past their Game 2 disappointment.

articles.title: Don Mattingly Named Phillies Manager on 2-Year Contract After MLB Rumors on Alex Cora Pursuit
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Phillies haved the interim tag and made Don Mattingly their full-time manager.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies haved the interim tag and made Don Mattingly their full-time manager.

Philadelphia confirmed the deal on Wednesday morning, noting Mattlingly's contract is for the 2027 and 2028 seasons.

Ranking Top 25 Trade Chips For Offseason 🔢

Matt Gelb and Charlotte Varnes of The Athletic first reported the decision.

Mattingly, 65, served as the Phillies' interim manager in 2026 after Rob Thomson was fired amid a 9-19 start. Philadelphia went 79-55 under Mattingly and reached the playoffs.

The Phillies are reportedly sticking with Mattingly after a failed attempt to court former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora, who told the organization last week that he does not want to manage in 2027, per Bob Nightengale of USA Today .

With Mattingly leading the way, the Phillies made their fifth consecutive playoff appearance, although they fell to the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card Series, marking their earliest playoff exit since the Wild Card Series was instituted.

Mattingly is best known for his legendary playing career, as "Donnie Baseball" spent 14 seasons with the New York Yankees, primarily as a first baseman.

For his career, he hit .307 with 222 home runs and 1,099 RBI, plus he was a six-time All-Star, nine-time Gold Glove Award winner, three-time Silver Slugger Award winner, one-time batting champion and one-time American League MVP.

Mattingly is also a highly experienced manager, having spent parts of 13 seasons in that role with the Los Angeles Dodgers, Miami Marlins and Phillies.

He has an overall record of 968-1,005 with five playoff appearances, plus he was named National League Manager of the Year in 2020 while with the Marlins.

The challenge for Mattingly moving forward in Philly will be getting the most out of a team whose key players are either exiting or already past their prime for the most part.

Designated hitter Kyle Schwarber, first baseman Bryce Harper, shortstop Trea Turner, catcher J.T. Realmuto and starting pitchers Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola are all at least 33 years old.

The Phillies do have some other notable players who are younger than that, including starting pitchers Cristopher Sánchez and Jesús Luzardo, outfielder Brandon Marsh and second baseman Bryson Stott.

However, remaining competitive in the NL against the likes of the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Braves and others could prove difficult as the Phillies' core continues to age out.

The organization apparently trusts Mattingly to get the most out of his players, though, on the heels of him turning around what was a nightmarish start to the 2026 campaign.

articles.title: Phillies expected to name Don Mattingly as full-time manager after 2026 turn around
articles.summary: Don Mattingly helped the Phillies recover from a terrible start in 2026.
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies got off to a miserable start in 2026, opening the season with a 9-19 record. The team acted swiftly amid its floundering, firing Rob Thomson and promoting Don Mattingly to be interim manager. Philadelphia immediately turned things around, going 79-55 the rest of the way and earning a playoff spot.

Because of that, Mattingly is expected to be named the team's full-time manager for 2027, according to The Athletic. The team is expected to make that announcement soon.

While Mattingly was credited with turning the Phillies' season around, his promotion to the full-time role was not a guarantee. The Phillies nearly blew a shot at the playoffs in September, going 3-6 over their final nine games to barely limp into the postseason. The team's poor performance then carried into the wild-card round, where the Phillies lost to the Atlanta Braves.

During the team's skid, Mattingly received criticism for his in-game strategy, particularly with his bullpen management.

Though Mattingly is expected to receive the full-time job, there's evidence he was not the Phillies' first choice. When Mattingly assumed the interim role in April, it was reported the team first reached out to former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora, who declined the job.

The Phillies reportedly reached out to Cora again after the 2026 season, but he once again refused the role .

That put the Phillies is a difficult spot moving foward. With a lockout expected this offseason due to the expiring collective-bargaining agreement (CBA), team personnel will not be allowed to communicate with players for — presumably — a large chunk of the winter. Those restrictions could make it tough on a new manager, who wouldn't be able to talk, strategize or get to know players amid a lockout. That will be less of an issue with Mattingly, who already has an established rapport with the team and its players.

Prior to managing the Phillies, Mattingly led both the Los Angeles Dodgers and Miami Marlins. His tenure with Los Angeles was far more successful, as he led the team to three postseason appearances in five seasons. He made the playoffs just once in seven seasons with Miami.

articles.title: Starting pitching targets for Padres this offseason
articles.summary: Who might San Diego try to sign?
articles.body:
Every time the offseason rolls around, the San Diego Padres seem to be in desperate need of starting pitching. Most of that is due to A.J. Preller's inability to sign a starter to a long-term contract. That should change this year, with San Diego only having three certain starters returning (Joe Musgrove, JP Sears and Randy Vásquez). For the sake of this exercise, I won't be including potential returners like Michael King ($28 million player option) or Nick Pivetta ($14 million club option).

Despite faltering from his 2024-25 Cy Young form, Skubal was still phenomenal in 2026. The southpaw dominated, posting a 2.72 ERA and 0.96 WHIP across 158 2/3 innings of work. Skubal will be the most sought after free agent on the market, pitcher or otherwise. Despite plenty of questions surrounding how the offseason may progress, Skubal is still set up for a big payday.

That's the big problem for San Diego signing him. Their coffers haven't been particualry deep in years past, but new ownership may change that. The question is whether it's worth it to make one big signing or several smaller ones. Skubal would implode any other potential to sign other marquee free agents. It might be better for the Friars to pursue two mid-tier options instead.

Rogers had an otherworldly 2025 campaign before majorly regressing this season. The southpaw posted a 1.81 ERA in '25 despite struggling to return from a right knee injury. Because of that, Rogers made just 18 starts (109.2 IP). He took a step back in '26 with a 4.03 ERA across 169 2/3 innings.

That said, the 29-year-old has his whole career ahead of him and could set up San Diego's rotation for years to come. The Padres haven't had a dominant starter from the left side of the mound in quite some time. However, the questions surrounding his health could hurt his case as a reliable pitcher to sign.

After being expected to retire for much of this season, Gray announced that he won't be leaving MLB quite so soon. The veteran right-hander desperately wants to win a World Series and would likely sign with a contending team, even if it was for less guaranteed dollars.

Gray is coming off of an incredible season with the Boston Red Sox (2.72 ERA, 169.0 IP). The question is if that dominance can continue. The 36-year-old hasn't proven his ability to be consistent in years past. Despite having five sub-3.00 ERA seasons in his career, none have ever been consecutive. Whether Gray can catch lightning in a bottle a second time remains to be seen until a team picks him up.

Griffin has drawn the spotlight lately after his heroics in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Tampa Bay Rays. After a shaky first inning, Griffin quieted the Rays for three more frames. The starter was traded from the Washington Nationals and has been a solid option in the Cleveland Guardians' rotation.

The 31-year-old finally got a shot in 2026 and ran with it. He pitched to a 3.60 ERA in 172 2/3 innings of work in his rookie season. Griffin was incredible during his earlier stint this year with Washington, but struggled once joining the Guards. If he's able to return to form in 2027, he could be a great value signing for the Padres.

The Chicago Cubs' left-hander has yet to replicate the beauty of his 2024 rookie season in MLB (2.91 ERA, 173.1 IP). He's still posted a sub-4.00 ERA in both 2025 (3.73 ERA) and 2026 (3.77 ERA), but they have certainly been a step back. However, Imanaga is coming off of a career-high innings pitched in 2026. That could be a massive addition for San Diego's pitching-hungry roster.

Imanaga also won't have a qualifying offer attached to him after rejecting the QO from Chicago last season. That means the Padres wouldn't need to give up a draft pick if they signed Imanaga. The Friars have plenty of options to turn to, but Imanaga could be a truly great move for San Diego to bolster their starting group.

Itoh will be the top free agent starting pitcher coming over from NPB in Japan. Across 1008 2/3 innings in Japanese professional baseball, the righty owns a 2.91 ERA. He's coming off of a relatively tougher year in 2026 with a 3.18 ERA across 172 2/3 innings pitched. Itoh has posted a sub-3.00 ERA in four of his last six years.

The righty pitched in both the 2023 and '26 World Baseball Classic. However, Itoh hasn't faced many major leaguers apart from his 6 1/3 innings between the two tournaments. That could make it tough for Itoh to adapt to MLB. But, he seems ready to make the transition, and has had proven success in Japan. The 29-year-old could be a huge boost for San Diego if he acclimates well to MLB.

articles.summary: Ohtani hasn't been fully healthy in quite some time — one reason for his struggles over the last few months.
articles.body:
Baseball's biggest superstar has looked anything but like one recently.

Shohei Ohtani 's 2026 season has been derailed over the last few months — after initially looking like he could contend for another NL MVP and Cy Young Award, pitching to a 1.79 ERA over 14 starts, he was first shut down as a pitcher in July.

Ohtani did later have an IL stint as he played through clear injury concerns, but came into the Dodgers' postseason run seemingly healthy enough to hit. It's been obvious on the big stage, though, that Ohtani isn't at 100%, so much so that the Dodgers reportedly began pondering benching him in the NLCS.

Here's what's known about Ohtani's injury concerns over the last few months.

Ohtani has been playing through health issues for months, though the Dodgers have been vague at times about the severity of those injuries.

After his incredible start to the season on the mound, Ohtani made his final start in early July, pulled against the Padres due to left knee discomfort and soreness in his right bicep. He missed the MLB All-Star Game due to those injuries — and initially, the Dodgers insisted he would return to his two-way talents, receiving a shot in his knee with other treatment to plan a return to the mound.

Instead, by early September, Ohtani was officially shut down as a pitcher, as the Dodgers announced he would focus on hitting for the remainder of the season due to his injury recovery not materializing as hoped.

Since then, even Ohtani as a hitter hasn't quite been the same elite threat. While he had a brief IL stint in September, he's been swinging through injury issues over the last few months.

Since at least June, Ohtani has been managing a left knee injury that led to him being shut down as a pitcher by July and put him on the 15-day IL in September.

The injuries haven't just resulted in his lack of two-way ability — Ohtani has not been the same elite hitter in a while.

According to MLB.com, as of Oct. 13, Ohtani was hitting .197 with a .629 OPS over his last 35 games, between the regular season and postseason. He last hit a home run on Aug. 18, only driving in one run since then; Ohtani's 110 plate appearances without a home run, including the postseason, are a career high.

"Yeah I mean obviously it hasn't been good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said during the NLCS, per MLB.com. "He doesn't feel great. I think for me, it's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it."

Ohtani's knee injury hasn't been officially described by the Dodgers as anything other than inflammation and soreness, though in 2019, he had season-ending surgery to repair a rare congenital condition called bipartite patella in the same knee. Ohtani previously told reporters that he "wonders" if his current knee issue is related to that surgery.

"It's more in the kneecap," Ohtani said in July, per the New York Post .

Part of the reason for Ohtani's struggles during his injuries is that it isn't just his knee — it's also his right bicep that has brought discomfort.

According to MLB.com, the bicep issue first affected Ohtani as a hitter in July, and it's lingered since, particularly when he was attempting to ramp back up for a return to the mound. By September, he reported to the team that it was still causing discomfort after taking a practice swing, which was right before he was then placed on the IL.

Paired with his knee issue, the bicep injury has added even more strain.

"Of course the best mode of recovery is to completely not play," Ohtani said through his interpreter at the time, per MLB.com . "But right now, I just want to make sure that I'm playing, playing well and just focusing on the now."

At this point, it's looking more like Ohtani will only be able to get back to 100% with a full offseason's rest, unable to get back up to full speed despite his IL stint. He will play in Game 3 against the Brewers after questions, per The Athletic , insisting that he's capable of being on the field.

"He was adamant that he can help us," Roberts said, per The Athletic. "He's well enough to help us win a baseball game, so that's all I needed to hear."

articles.title: NLCS notes: Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani’s status for Game 3
articles.summary: For the first time in five years, the Dodgers find themselves down two games to begin the National League Championship Series with the series headed back to...
articles.body:
For the first time in five years, the Dodgers find themselves down two games to begin the National League Championship Series with the series headed back to Los Angeles.

The Dodgers offense has shown little to no fight in the series, with Game 2's back-and-forth clash being the most exhilarating matchup so far. Their duo of bona fide aces, Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto, have combined for just 7 2/3 innings on the mound while surrendering five earned runs.

Now the Dodgers will rely on both Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow to try and keep the chances at a three peat alive. Snell was shaky at best in his most recent outing against the Atlanta Braves, tossing 90 pitches over just 3 2/3 innings. Snell may have the pedigree from previous performances in the postseason, but his sole focus is the here and now in trying to lift the Dodgers from a two-game deficit, per Christina De Nicola of MLB.com .

"I don't think about last year because it has nothing to do with this year," Snell said. "It's a completely different team. … This game and what it means to me, it hasn't changed — 0-2, 2-0, it wouldn't matter. I know what I need to do. I know what I need to do to win and dominate. I'm going to just focus on that."

In preparation for his start on Wednesday, Snell has noticed the small details that occur within and outside the Brewers' dugout, per Thomas L. Murray of the California Post .

"I noticed how they talk, a lot of one-on-one competition is a key for them. The way Pat Murphy talks to the team is way different than last year," Snell said. "So I understand that."

Shohei Ohtani has endured in a nightmare of a postseason so far, going as far down as fifth in the lineup while struggling to the tune of a .150/.261/.150 slash line over six games. This slump has warranted Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times to suggest that Ohtani be removed from the lineup completely, as he demands in his latest column.

articles.title: World Series 2026 Updated Bracket Predictions Before Rays vs. Guardians ALCS Game 3
articles.summary: The 2026 ALCS is now a best-of-five.
articles.body:
After the Cleveland Guardians grabbed Game 1, the Tampa Bay Rays recovered to take Game 2 on Tuesday. With the series shifting to Cleveland for Game 3, things are knotted at 1-1, putting both clubs three victories away from a World Series trip.

It should be a nail-biter moving forward, as these teams might be too similar for either to separate. What they lack in payroll and name recognition, they more than make up for in fundamentals, contact, chaos-creation on the basepaths and all-the-little-things small ball.

Stylistic clashes can be great to watch this time of year, but it's hard to beat watching a team effectively trying to conquer its mirror image.

Game 3: Rays at Guardians, 6 p.m. ET on TBS/truTV

Game 4: Rays at Guardians, 6 p.m. ET on TBS/truTV*

Game 5: Rays at Guardians, 8 p.m. ET on TBS/truTV

Game 6: Guardians at Rays, 5 p.m. ET on TBS/truTV* (if necessary)

Game 7: Guardians at Rays, 8 p.m. ET on TBS/truTV (if necessary)

*Game time would change to 8 p.m. ET if NLCS is finished.

Cleveland's pitchers finished Game 2 without a single earned run allowed. So, how did this team drop a 3-1 contest?

It all had to do with Guardians star third baseman José Ramírez and his uncharacteristically rough fourth inning. He followed a mental mistake with a fielding error, allowing the Rays to plate all three of their unearned runs.

"It's frustrating," Ramírez told reporters through an interpreter. "I feel bad because I wasn't able to make that play and after that the runs came in. I feel bad about that."

Ramírez's teammates surely reminded him they'd never be in this position without him. He might have been due for some stumbles after engineering a legendary run between Cleveland's ALDS comeback and ALCS Game 1 victory, tallying eight hits, eight RBI, seven runs scored and two home runs over that four-game stretch.

A Guardians' path to victory starts with following Ramírez's and getting more great innings out of Gavin Williams (1.54 ERA with 24 strikeouts in 11.2 innings this postseason). Play sound defense, pressure the opponents with contact and speed, and that's the blueprint for victory.

Of course, it's basically the same one used by Tampa, which is turning to Griffin Jax for the Game 3 start after he was only needed for relief work in its sweep of the New York Yankees. But the Rays also must find a way to activate star slugger Junior Caminero, who had 42 homers and 101 RBI in the regular season but is homerless with a single RBI through five playoff games so far.

While no one should discount the Los Angeles Dodgers and their ability to do...well, anything, it'd be hard to take them over the Milwaukee Brewers right now. Climbing out of an 0-2 hole is always tricky, but it sounds like a nightmarish task against a 103-win team.

So, our crystal ball is ready to pencil the Brewers into the championship round. But who will meet them there?

The Guardians would be a great story. They last won a World Series in 1948. They were pushed to the brink by the White Sox before recovering just in time to win three straight had-to-have-them games. Save for Ramírez, they lack recognizable stars, but they know how to win without them.

The problem is the Rays are just a better team. The better team may not always come out on top, but it's usually the smart one to pick.

Cleveland was above-average this season (85 wins, plus-11 run differential); Tampa Bay was terrific (98 wins, plus-86). The Rays have a real masher in their lineup with Junior Caminero, but they also have depth, speed and contact. They pitch and defend, too.

The Guardians look good, but the Rays look a better version of the same team. Look for Tampa to secure its spot alongside Milwaukee in the World Series.

articles.title: Joe Espada Dismissed as Astros Manager Amid Mariners Links in New MLB Rumors
articles.summary: The Houston Astros are parting ways with Joe Espada amid rumors of his candidacy for the Seattle Mariners' managerial opening.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros are parting ways with Joe Espada amid rumors of his candidacy for the Seattle Mariners' managerial opening.

The Astros announced Espada's exit Wednesday, two weeks after the club was swept from the Wild Card round by the Chicago White Sox.

Espada had served as the Astros' bench coach from 2018 to 2023 before taking over as manager ahead of the 2024 season.

His contract is set to expire at the end of October and will not be renewed, according to the Astros .

Espada will leave the Astros having compiled a 256-229 regular-season record and two AL West titles while going winless in two Wild Card appearances.

His departure will allow the Astros' next general manager to start over with a new coaching staff. The organization already parted ways with former general manager Dana Brown in August.

The Astros qualified for the postseason after winning the division, but their 81-81 record marked a fourth straight season of declining win totals following the club's run to the 2022 World Series title.

Whichever leaders are hired to replace Brown and Espada will be tasked with deciding whether the Astros need to begin a roster teardown in order to rebuild their farm system or can retool with offseason additions with hope of making a deeper postseason run next spring.

The Astros are the second club this offseason to make a managerial change. The Mariners got the carousel started by parting ways with former manager Dan Wilson after falling short of the 2026 postseason.

MLB Network's Jon Heyman and Mark Feinsand reported Tuesday Espada was "among possible candidates who'd fit preference for experience" in Seattle.

The Astros had already granted the Mariners permission to speak to Espada, who had a meeting scheduled with Seattle prior to the club announcing his exit, MLB.com's Feinsand, Daniel Kramer and Brian McTaggart reported.

Heyman also named former Minnesota Twins manager and current Los Angeles Dodgers executive Rocco Baldelli, former Baltimore Orioles manager and current Tampa Bay Rays executive Brandon Hyde, and former Chicago Cubs manager David Ross as possible candidates for the Mariners job.

Whether the Mariners ultimately consider any of these options could determine whether the Astros watch Espada head to an AL West rival this offseason.

articles.title: Rays vs. Guardians ALCS Game 3 Rescheduled by MLB Due to Inclement Weather, Latest Forecast
articles.summary: MLB announced it's moving up the start for Game 3 of the American League Championship Series due to inclement weather forecast for Cleveland.
articles.body:
MLB announced it's moving up the start for Game 3 of the American League Championship Series due to inclement weather forecast for Cleveland.

The first pitch will be 1 p.m. ET instead of 6 p.m.

According to The Weather Channel , the rain isn't expected until 11 p.m. ET on Thursday, but there's clearly a fear the front will move in earlier than that.

MLB hasn't yet made any changes to Game 4 on Friday, which could be in more jeopardy. The forecast calls for scattered thunderstorms in the morning and rain into the evening.

Should Game 4 get postponed, the weather should clear up Saturday, and the teams have a day off on Sunday that could serve as a makeup date.

Moving an ALCS game to a weekday afternoon is obviously not ideal for those who have tickets. Be prepared to call off work or get an excuse to skip class.

By taking this step, though, MLB is basically saying it didn't see an alternative.

The ALCS is tied heading to Progressive Field after the Tampa Bay Rays earned a 3-1 win in Game 2 on Tuesday night.

articles.title: Guardians-Rays ALCS Game 3 start time moved up to 1 p.m. ET due to rain in the forecast
articles.summary: The Rays evened the series at one with a 3-1 win on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
Thursday's Game 3 of the 2026 ALCS between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays has been moved up from a 6 p.m. ET start to 1 p.m. ET, MLB announced.

The game at Progressive Field in Cleveland will see an earlier start due to the rain forecast on Thursday night in the area.

The Guardians and Rays are tied 1-1 in the best-of-7 series following Tampa's 3-1 win on Tuesday night.

Freddy Peralta continued to dominate on the mound for the Rays since being dealt from the New York Mets. The right-hander went six innings, allowed zero runs and struck out six. Over his last eight appearances, he has recorded a 0.81 ERA.

Game 3, which will air on TBS, HBO MAX, and TruTV, will feature Griffin Jax on the mound for the Rays and Gavin Williams likely going for the Guardians.

"It's going to be a challenging place to play," said Rays manager Kevin Cash. "We played there not too long ago in the postseason. That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see. They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team. I'd like to think we can carry our momentum into there and just play good baseball for Game 3."

Cleveland-Tampa will be the first of two games Thursday. Game 4 of the Milwaukee Brewers-Los Angeles Dodges NLCS will start at 9 p.m. ET from Dodger Stadium.

articles.title: Houston Astros part ways with manager Joe Espada in franchise reset that could mark end of era
articles.summary: The news arrives a day after a report surfaced that Espada was granted permission to interview for the Seattle Mariners' manager position.
articles.body:
The Houston Astros have parted ways with manager Joe Espada, the team announced Wednesday. The news arrived a day after a report surfaced that Espada was granted permission to interview for the Seattle Mariners' manager position .

While the Astros are moving on from Espada, they also revealed Wednesday that they're retaining pitching coach Josh Miller, first-base coach Dave Clark, field coordinator Jason Bell, hitting coach Victor Rodriguez and bullpen catcher Javier Bracamonte. Plus, per the team, bench coach Omar Lopez has been offered an opportunity to remain with the organization in a new role.

During Espada's three seasons at the helm, Houston went 256-229. In that span, the Astros never won more than 88 games in a season. Conversely, they didn't finish one of those campaigns below .500. Despite a horde of injuries and questionable front-office decisions, Espada's Astros reached the postseason twice.

Their resilience turned heads, particularly when they rebounded from a 12-24 start in 2024 to win the American League West crown, and when they began this season 20-31 before scrounging together the pieces to field a division-winning squad, albeit in a historically weak AL West this time around .

Yet Espada-led Houston teams didn't fare well in the playoffs. They went a combined 0-4, bowing out in the wild-card round both times. This season, the Astros were swept by the upstart Chicago White Sox . Even though Houston was at home for each game of the series, it didn't lead once. Daikin Park didn't sell out for either matchup, and Astros fans didn't hold back their frustration toward the team in Game 1. After the series-opening defeat, multiple players conveyed their disappointment in the boos they heard, although left-handed relief pitcher Bennett Sousa ultimately apologized for his comments about the fan base .

An Astros pitching staff — ravaged by injury and poorly constructed from the outset — dug the team holes against the White Sox that were too deep for even Houston's power-surged bats to lift the group out of the jaws of defeat.

No team hit more home runs this season than the Astros, who wrapped the regular season with 226 dingers, in part thanks to AL MVP favorite Yordan Alvarez and his 42 long balls. The problem was that Houston was responsible for the seventh-worst ERA (4.45) in the bigs.

Astros owner Jim Crane said in August, according to The Athletic , that Espada was "doing what he can do with what he's got." That remark was made in the wake of Crane firing beleaguered general manager Dana Brown .

Brown entered the 2026 campaign in the final year of his contract, as did Espada. Brown's offseason was much maligned. The Astros didn't wind up with convincing answers to their outfield questions, and the arms he brought in floundered. Namely, former Nippon Professional Baseball standout Tatsuya Imai struggled mightily, as the righty fell out of Houston's starting rotation.

Espada, 51, was regarded as a players' manager throughout his time leading the Astros' clubhouse. Before landing the skipper gig, he spent six seasons as a bench coach for the club, working under A.J. Hinch and Dusty Baker.

His removal is part of a franchise reset that could mark the end of an era for Houston, which won its first two World Series titles in 2017 and 2022 and has made the postseason nine of the past 10 seasons.

articles.title: PCA, Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Bobby Witt Headline Full List of 2026 MLB Gold Glove Award Finalists
articles.summary: Some of the best defensive players in baseball are one step closer to a Gold Glove.
articles.body:
Some of the best defensive players in baseball are one step closer to a Gold Glove.

The Gold Glove finalists were announced Wednesday, and superstars such as Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bobby Witt and Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among others, jump out from the list .

There are three finalists at each position for each league, and the winners will be announced Nov. 1 during an ESPN broadcast. Here is a look at all the finalists on a position-by-position basis.

Ranking Top 25 Trade Chips For Offseason 🔢

José Soriano, Los Angeles Angels/Toronto Blue Jays

Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Toronto Blue Jays

Now that the finalists have been announced, attention also turns to the Platinum Glove race.

That goes to the single best defender in each league, and Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller predicted the honors will go to Crow-Armstrong in the National League and Witt in the American League.

Crow-Armstrong's position as the favorite underscores his ability to impact the game in so many ways and why he will, in all likelihood, be the National League MVP as well.

After all, he went 40/40 on the offensive side with 45 home runs, 41 stolen bases and 107 RBI while also leading the league with 119 runs scored. That his defense may be even better than his offense is a testament to his work with the glove.

According to Statcast , he led all of baseball with 26 outs above average. The next-closest outfielder was Ceddanne Rafaela of the Boston Red Sox with 17.

What's more, Crow-Armstrong caught 50 percent of his 5-star catch opportunities, which was the best mark in the league on the most difficult hit balls to catch. He likely would have seen even more 5-star chances if he didn't make plays that would be so difficult for others rather routine with his speed.

He won the American League Platinum Glove last season and is a back-to-back Gold Glove winner at shortstop. He finished with the best outs above average total in the American League with 24.

That was well ahead of Andrés Giménez of the Toronto Blue Jays, who was second at 19. Notably, they both play shortstop.

If Giménez played a different position, he could be a near lock to win a Gold Glove. Instead, he has to compete with the best defender in the American League in Witt.

And it would be anything but surprising if Witt was recognized accordingly for the second straight year.
